name: Reign of Justinian
summary: The Byzantine emperor Justinian I codified Roman law, rebuilt Hagia Sophia, and briefly reconquered Italy, North Africa and southern Spain.
body:
Justinian I ruled the eastern Roman empire from Constantinople for thirty-eight years, from 527 to 565. He had Roman law gathered and rewritten as the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, rebuilt [Hagia Sophia](event:hagia-sophia), and sent his armies to [recover the western provinces](event:justinian-wars) lost to the Vandals and the Goths. His reign is usually treated as the last serious attempt to restore the Roman empire as a Mediterranean whole.

He came to the throne as the nephew and heir of the emperor Justin I, and governed alongside his wife Theodora, whose influence contemporaries thought decisive, most visibly during the Nika riots of 532, when much of Constantinople burned and the emperor considered flight. The rebuilding of the capital, and the churches and frontier fortifications raised across the empire, were paid for by heavy taxation gathered by ministers such as John the Cappadocian.

The legal work proved the most durable part. A commission under the jurist Tribonian compressed centuries of imperial edicts and juristic writing into a code, a digest, a students' textbook and a body of new laws. Rediscovered in eleventh-century Italy, it became the foundation of the civil law tradition in continental Europe and Latin America.

The reconquest did not hold. The Italian war lasted almost twenty years and wrecked the peninsula, war with Sasanian Persia ran on in the east, and the [plague](event:justinian-plague) of 541 took the taxpayers and soldiers the effort depended on. Most of the western gains were lost within a generation of his death.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I).

name: Justinian's reconquest wars
summary: Justinian's armies reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of southern Spain from the Vandal and Gothic kingdoms.
body:
Part of [Reign of Justinian](event:justinian). Justinian sent his armies west to take back provinces the Roman empire had lost to Germanic kingdoms in the previous century. Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom of North Africa in a single campaign in 533–534, then landed in Sicily and began a war for Italy against the Ostrogoths that ran until 554. A smaller expedition took a strip of southern Spain from the Visigoths in 552.

The African war was quick; the Italian one was not. Rome changed hands several times, the Gothic king Totila recovered most of the peninsula in the 540s, and the war was only finished by the eunuch general Narses at Taginae and Mons Lactarius in 552–553. Italy emerged depopulated, with its aqueducts cut and its senate gone. The Pragmatic Sanction of 554 imposed imperial administration on what was left.

The empire could not hold the gains. War with Sasanian Persia on the eastern frontier and the [plague of 541](event:justinian-plague) drained men and money faster than the west could repay them. Lombard invaders took most of Italy from 568, the Visigoths recovered the Spanish coast by 624, and North Africa stayed imperial only until the [Arab conquests](event:islamic-conquests) of the 690s.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_War_(535%E2%80%93554)).

name: Hagia Sophia completed
summary: Justinian's domed church in Constantinople was completed in 537, and held the largest enclosed space in the world for nearly a thousand years.
body:
Part of [Reign of Justinian](event:justinian). Hagia Sophia, the Church of the Holy Wisdom, was completed in Constantinople in 537 after five years of building. Its dome, about 31 metres across and carried on pendentives over a square hall, covered the largest enclosed space in the world, and no larger one was built for nearly a thousand years. It was the principal church of the eastern empire and the setting of imperial ceremony.

Justinian ordered it after the previous church on the site burned in the Nika riots of 532, and gave the design to two men described in the sources as *mechanikoi* rather than as builders: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. A ring of forty windows at the base of the dome makes the vault appear to rest on light, an effect contemporaries wrote about at length. The first dome was too shallow and fell after earthquakes in 558; the steeper replacement, finished in 562, is substantially what stands today.

After the [Ottoman capture of the city](event:fall-constantinople) in 1453 the building became a mosque, and minarets, buttresses and calligraphic roundels were added. It was made a museum in 1935 and returned to use as a mosque in 2020.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia).

name: Plague of Justinian
summary: The first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague broke out in 541 and recurred around the Mediterranean for two centuries.
body:
Part of [Reign of Justinian](event:justinian). The Plague of Justinian was the first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague. It broke out in Roman Egypt in 541, reached Constantinople the same year and spread around the Mediterranean by 544, and opened what historians call the first plague pandemic, whose waves recurred until the middle of the eighth century. The same bacterium, *Yersinia pestis*, caused the [Black Death](event:black-death) eight centuries later; DNA recovered from sixth-century graves confirmed this in 2013.

The court historian Procopius described the outbreak in Constantinople closely, including the swellings, the delirium and the collapse of any orderly burial. Justinian himself caught the disease and recovered. The death toll is genuinely disputed. Older estimates put it at anything from 15 to 100 million across the two centuries of recurrence; more recent work, reading grave archaeology, coin finds and pollen records, argues that mortality outside the crowded ports may have been far lower than the written sources suggest.

The timing is less disputed than the scale. The plague struck in the middle of [Justinian's reconquest](event:justinian-wars), while the empire was already fighting in Italy and against Persia, and it kept returning for as long as the effort lasted.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_of_Justinian).

name: Tang dynasty
summary: A cosmopolitan Chinese golden age of poetry, Buddhism and long-distance trade, with Chang'an the largest city on Earth.
body:
The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907. Its capital Chang'an, at the eastern end of the [Silk Road](event:silk-road), was the largest city in the world and held foreign merchants, monks and envoys in numbers no earlier Chinese capital had seen. The period is conventionally treated as a high point of Chinese poetry, Buddhism and long-distance trade.

The Li family founded the dynasty on the ruins of the short-lived Sui, and it reached its greatest extent under Taizong and Xuanzong, with garrisons deep into Central Asia. Government ran through a mature bureaucracy in which the imperial examinations, though still less important than aristocratic connection, were becoming a route to office. Wu Zetian, the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name, held power for much of the late seventh century.

Li Bai and Du Fu wrote in this period, [woodblock printing](event:woodblock-printing) appeared, and the Chan school of Buddhism took the form later carried to Korea and Japan. Buddhist monasteries grew rich enough to be suppressed and stripped of land in 845.

The An Lushan rebellion of 755–763 wrecked the dynasty's finances and its hold on the provinces, and the last century of Tang rule belonged to regional military governors. The empire broke up in 907 and was reassembled by the [Song](event:song-dynasty) in 960.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty).

name: The Hijra and the founding of Islam
summary: Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, founding the first Muslim community; the year is year one of the Islamic calendar.
body:
In 622 Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for the oasis town of Yathrib, afterwards called Medina, following years of hostility from the Meccan leadership. The migration, the *hijra*, is the event from which the Islamic calendar counts its years. At Medina the community became a political body as well as a religious one, with Muhammad as its leader and arbitrator.

Muhammad had begun preaching in Mecca around 610, teaching the oneness of God, the duty of charity and a coming judgement, in a city whose trade and standing rested partly on pilgrimage to its shrines. His followers were a small and increasingly harassed minority, and some had already taken refuge in Christian Ethiopia. An invitation from clans at Yathrib, who wanted an outside arbitrator for their own long feud, gave the community somewhere to go.

The Medinan decade produced practices central to Islam since: communal prayer, the fast of Ramadan, the alms tax and the direction of prayer turned toward Mecca. It also produced a running conflict with the Meccans that ended with the surrender of Mecca in 630. By Muhammad's death in 632 most of the Arabian peninsula had accepted his authority.

The revelations he recited were collected as the Quran within a generation. His successors, the caliphs, disagreed over who had the right to lead, a dispute that separated Sunni and Shia Islam. Within a century their armies ruled from Spain to the Indus (see the [early Muslim conquests](event:islamic-conquests)). Islam is today the second largest religion in the world, with about 1.9 billion adherents.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah).

name: Early Muslim conquests
summary: Arab armies took Persia, the Levant, Egypt, North Africa and most of Spain within roughly a century of Muhammad's death.
body:
Part of [The Hijra and the founding of Islam](event:hijra). In the century after Muhammad's death in 632, armies from Arabia destroyed the Sasanian empire outright and took the southern and eastern provinces of Byzantium, then North Africa and most of the Iberian peninsula. It was one of the fastest territorial expansions in recorded history: from the Arabian peninsula to an empire reaching from the Atlantic to the Indus.

Both of the powers the Arabs faced had just fought each other to exhaustion in a war lasting from 602 to 628, and neither could replace a lost field army quickly. The Arab forces were mobile, unified under the authority of the caliphs at Medina and later the Umayyads at Damascus, and willing to campaign far from home. Persia was conquered entirely; Byzantium survived behind the Taurus mountains but lost Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa, and never recovered them.

Conquest was not conversion. Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians who submitted kept their religion and paid a poll tax, and for the first century Muslims were a ruling minority living largely in new garrison towns such as Basra, Kufa and Fustat. Conversion of the conquered populations happened slowly, over several centuries.

The advance stopped at recognisable limits: the Anatolian plateau and the walls of Constantinople in the north, the Pyrenees and the Franks at [Tours](event:tours) in the west, the mountains and deserts of the Indian and Central Asian frontiers in the east. The Umayyad caliphate that had assembled it was overthrown by the Abbasids in 750, and the empire began to divide into separate states.

The campaigns ran in distinct phases, listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests).

steps.name: The Ridda wars
steps.page: Muhammad's death in 632 left it unclear whether the tribes of Arabia had submitted to him personally or to the community he led. Several repudiated Medina's authority, and some followed rival prophets. The first caliph, Abu Bakr, spent a year forcing them back by arms. The wars ended with Arabia unified under Medina and with an army in the field that had nowhere left to fight.

steps.name: Into Syria and Iraq
steps.page: Columns sent north from Medina raided the Byzantine border provinces and the Sasanian lands of lower Iraq at the same time. Damascus fell in 634. Khalid ibn al-Walid marched a force across the desert from Iraq to Syria to join the western campaign, a move the sources treat as the decisive stroke of the war.

steps.name: The fall of Sasanian Persia
steps.page: The victory at al-Qadisiyyah in 636 opened Mesopotamia and the Sasanian capital of Ctesiphon. The Persian army was broken again at Nahavand in 642, after which the empire was taken province by province. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed in flight near Merv in 651. Unlike Byzantium, the Sasanian state did not survive at all.

steps.name: Egypt and Alexandria
steps.page: Amr ibn al-As entered Egypt in 639 with a small force, took the fortress of Babylon on the Nile in 641 and accepted the surrender of Alexandria in 642. He founded a garrison town, Fustat, beside the fortress; Cairo later grew from it. Egypt's grain, which had fed Constantinople, now fed the caliphate.

steps.name: Across North Africa
steps.page: The advance west was slower, fought against Byzantine garrisons and against Berber confederations who resisted for decades. Qayrawan was founded as a base in 670, Carthage taken in 698, and the Atlantic coast reached by about 709. Berber converts made up much of the army that crossed into Spain.

steps.name: Al-Andalus
steps.page: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait in 711 with a mainly Berber force and destroyed the Visigothic king Roderic's army. The kingdom collapsed quickly and most of the peninsula was under Muslim rule by 718. Christian resistance survived in the northern mountains, which is where the [Reconquista](event:reconquista) begins.

name: Battle of Yarmouk
summary: An Arab victory over the main Byzantine field army in 636 opened Syria and Palestine to Muslim rule.
body:
Part of [Early Muslim conquests](event:islamic-conquests). The Battle of Yarmouk was fought in August 636 near the Yarmouk river, on the frontier of present-day Syria and Jordan, between the Arab Muslim army and the main Byzantine field force. The Arabs won decisively. Byzantium lost the army with which it might have held Syria, and the province passed to Muslim rule within a few years.

The emperor Heraclius had recovered Syria from the Persians only a few years earlier, at the end of a war that had lasted a generation. The force he assembled against the Arab advance was large. The figures in the sources are unreliable, but it was probably the bigger army, and it was drawn from contingents that co-operated badly. The Arab commanders, among them Khalid ibn al-Walid, fought a battle lasting several days on broken ground between ravines and broke the Byzantine line.

Heraclius withdrew to Antioch and then to Constantinople, abandoning Syria; the empire pulled back behind the Taurus mountains, which stayed its frontier for the next three centuries. Jerusalem surrendered soon after, in 637 or 638.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Yarmuk).

name: The Reconquista
summary: Christian kingdoms expanded across the Iberian peninsula at the expense of Muslim al-Andalus over nearly eight centuries, ending at Granada in 1492.
body:
Reconquista is the name later historians gave to the long process by which the Christian kingdoms of northern Iberia expanded southward at the expense of Muslim al-Andalus, between the eighth century and 1492. It was not one continuous war. Long periods of coexistence, tribute and cross-border alliance alternated with bursts of conquest, and the Christian kingdoms fought each other about as often as they fought Muslim ones.

Muslim armies had taken almost the whole peninsula by 718. Small Christian polities survived in the Cantabrian mountains and the Pyrenees and grew into the kingdoms of Asturias-León, Castile, Navarre, Aragon and Portugal. The frontier moved south in stages, each of them following the political collapse of a Muslim state: the break-up of the caliphate of Córdoba into taifa kingdoms after 1031, and the later failure of the Almoravid and Almohad empires brought over from North Africa. Settlers, military orders and royal charters filled the ground behind each advance.

The term itself is a modern one. Medieval writers did not use it, and its framing of eight centuries as a single Christian recovery was consolidated in Spanish historiography only in the nineteenth century, carrying political freight that historians now treat with care.

The conquest of [Granada](event:granada) in January 1492 ended Muslim rule in Iberia. The same monarchs expelled Spain's Jews that year and sponsored [Columbus](event:columbus); the remaining Muslims were forced to convert or leave over the following century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista).

steps.name: Battle of Covadonga
steps.page: A Muslim column sent into the Asturian mountains was beaten by a band under Pelagius, in a skirmish that later chroniclers turned into a founding victory. Dated to about 718 or 722, it marks the survival of a Christian polity in the north, the kingdom of Asturias, rather than the start of any reconquest campaign.

steps.name: The caliphate of Córdoba breaks up
steps.page: The Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba, the strongest state in the peninsula, dissolved after a long civil war into some three dozen taifa kingdoms. Divided and wealthy, they bought protection from the Christian kingdoms with tribute in gold, which financed the armies that later took their territory.

steps.name: Alfonso VI takes Toledo
steps.page: Alfonso VI of León and Castile took Toledo, the old Visigothic capital, and pushed the frontier to the Tagus. The taifa kings called in the Almoravids of Morocco, who stopped the Christian advance at Sagrajas in 1086 and then annexed the taifas themselves. Toledo's libraries and its mixed population of Arabic, Latin and Hebrew readers made it the main channel through which Arabic learning reached Latin Europe.

steps.name: Las Navas de Tolosa
steps.page: A combined army of Castile, Aragon and Navarre, raised as a crusade, broke the Almohad field army in the Sierra Morena. Almohad power in the peninsula collapsed within a generation and the passes into Andalusia lay open.

steps.name: Córdoba and Seville
steps.page: Ferdinand III of Castile took Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248; James I of Aragon took Valencia in 1238 and the Balearics in the 1230s; Portugal reached the Algarve in 1249. Muslim Iberia was reduced to the emirate of Granada, which survived for a further two and a half centuries as a tributary of Castile.

steps.name: The war for Granada
steps.page: Ferdinand and Isabella, having joined Castile and Aragon by marriage, spent ten years reducing the emirate town by town with siege artillery and blockade, helped by a civil war inside the Nasrid family. Málaga fell in 1487, Baza in 1489, and the capital was surrounded in 1491.

name: Battle of Tours
summary: Charles Martel's Franks halted an Umayyad raiding army between Tours and Poitiers in 732.
body:
Part of [Early Muslim conquests](event:islamic-conquests). At Tours, or Poitiers (the sources place the site between the two), in October 732 a Frankish army under Charles Martel defeated an Umayyad force raiding north from al-Andalus. The governor of Spain, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, was killed and the raid turned back. The battle is traditionally taken to mark the northern limit of the Muslim advance into western Europe.

Arab and Berber armies in Spain had been raiding across the Pyrenees into Aquitaine for a decade. This expedition sacked Bordeaux and was moving on the rich shrine of St Martin at Tours when Duke Odo of Aquitaine appealed to the Franks. Martel, then the effective ruler of the Frankish kingdoms as mayor of the palace, met it with an infantry force that held formation against cavalry charges for a day.

Later tradition, from Edward Gibbon onward, made the battle the moment Europe was saved for Christianity. Modern historians treat it more narrowly: it stopped a raid rather than an invasion, and Muslim forces held Narbonne until 759. Its importance for the Franks themselves is clearer: it added to Martel's prestige and helped his family, the Carolingians, replace the Merovingian kings a generation later under [Charlemagne](event:charlemagne).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tours).

name: Harun al-Rashid's reign
summary: The fifth Abbasid caliph ruled from Baghdad at the height of the dynasty's wealth, patronising scholarship and exchanging embassies with Charlemagne.
body:
Part of [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age). Harun al-Rashid was the fifth Abbasid caliph, ruling from 786 to 809 at the height of the dynasty's wealth and reach. His court, at Baghdad and later at Raqqa on the Euphrates, supported poets, musicians, jurists and translators, and exchanged embassies and gifts with Charlemagne in the west and the Tang court in the east. He is also the caliph of the *Thousand and One Nights*, a literary figure with only a loose relation to the ruler.

The empire he inherited ran from North Africa to Central Asia and was administered for much of his reign by the Barmakid family of viziers, whom he destroyed in 803 for reasons the sources do not agree on. Tax revenue from Iraq's irrigated farmland paid for a standing army, a postal and intelligence service, and building on a large scale. Campaigns against Byzantium were nearly annual and fought mainly for tribute and prestige.

The translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic was already under way in his reign, and was institutionalised by his son al-Ma'mun in the House of Wisdom (see the [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age)).

He divided the succession between two sons, which produced a civil war after his death in 809 from which the central authority of the caliphate never fully recovered.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harun_al-Rashid).

name: Islamic Golden Age
summary: Baghdad, Córdoba and Cairo led the world in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy for roughly five centuries.
body:
The Islamic Golden Age is the name given to a long period, conventionally from the eighth century to the thirteenth, in which scholarship in the Islamic world led the world in mathematics, astronomy, medicine, optics, geography and philosophy. Its centres were Baghdad under the Abbasids, Córdoba in al-Andalus and Cairo under the Fatimids. Its common language was Arabic, and its scholars were Muslims, Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians.

It began with translation. Greek, Persian, Syriac and Indian texts were rendered into Arabic on a large scale from the late eighth century, gathered in Baghdad at the library and translation circle remembered as the House of Wisdom, and paid for by caliphs, viziers and private patrons. Paper, a technique learned from China in the eighth century, made books far cheaper than parchment ever had.

Translation turned into research. [Al-Khwarizmi](event:al-khwarizmi) set out algebra as a subject in its own right; Ibn al-Haytham established that vision works by light entering the eye, and argued it from controlled experiment; al-Biruni measured the size of the Earth; [Ibn Sina's](item:ibn-sina) *Canon* organised medicine into a system; teaching hospitals were founded in the major cities.

Much of this learning entered Latin Europe through the translation centres of Toledo and Sicily from the twelfth century, where it fed [scholasticism](event:scholasticism) and the new [universities](event:university-bologna). The conventional end date is the Mongol [sack of Baghdad](event:baghdad-1258) in 1258, though scholarship continued in Cairo, Iran, Central Asia and al-Andalus long after it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Golden_Age).

name: Viking Age
summary: Scandinavian raiders, traders and settlers ranged from Newfoundland to Baghdad for nearly three centuries.
body:
The Viking Age is the period, conventionally from the 790s to about 1066, in which Scandinavians raided, traded and settled across Europe and the North Atlantic. They reached Newfoundland in the west and the Caspian and Baghdad in the east, and left permanent settlements in England, Ireland, Scotland, Normandy, Iceland and the Rus' lands.

Why it began is debated: better ships, population pressure at home, the wealth of undefended coastal monasteries, and the closing of other trade routes have all been argued. The ships are certain. The clinker-built longship could cross open sea and then be rowed up a river or run onto a beach, which put almost any settlement in northern Europe within reach of an armed crew.

Raiding turned into settlement. Danish armies wintered in England from 865 and took much of it as the Danelaw; Norse settlers founded Dublin and other Irish ports, colonised Iceland from about 870 and Greenland from 985, and briefly reached [Vinland](event:vinland). Swedish traders on the Russian rivers dealt in furs, slaves and silver as far as the Abbasid caliphate, and were bound up with the founding of Kyiv and Novgorod. In 911 a Norse band was granted the land that became Normandy.

The age closed as Scandinavia became Christian and centralised under kings, and its rulers were absorbed into the politics of Christian Europe. The Normans [conquered England](event:hastings) in 1066.

The course of the age is traced in the steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Age).

steps.name: Four decades of raiding
steps.page: For two generations the pattern was the summer raid: a few ships, a coastal monastery or a trading place, and a return home before winter. Iona was attacked repeatedly from 795, Ireland from the same decade, and the Frankish empire's river valleys from the 830s, when the Carolingian succession disputes left the coasts unwatched. Paris was ransomed in 845. Norse crews founded fortified harbours in Ireland, Dublin from 841, that were bases first and towns afterwards.

steps.name: The rivers to Byzantium and Baghdad
steps.page: Scandinavians the Greeks called Rus' worked the rivers of eastern Europe, portaging between the Volga, the Dnieper and the Baltic, and dealt in furs, wax, honey and slaves. Arab silver from the Abbasid caliphate came back in such quantity that hoards of it are the largest source of Islamic coins anywhere. Novgorod and Kyiv grew from their trading centres, and the dynasty conventionally dated from Rurik in 862 became the rulers of the Kyivan Rus'. Fleets attacked Constantinople several times; survivors of them ended up as the emperor's Varangian guard.

steps.name: The Great Heathen Army
steps.page: In 865 an army landed in East Anglia that did not go home. Over the following decade it destroyed the kingdoms of Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia, and only Wessex under Alfred survived, at Edington in 878. The land the Danes settled became known as the Danelaw, and its place-names, legal terms and vocabulary are still in the English language and on the English map.

steps.name: The settlement of Iceland
steps.page: An uninhabited island was settled from Norway and from the Norse colonies in the British Isles within about sixty years, the *Landnámabók* naming some four hundred original settlers. The assembly the settlers established at Thingvellir, the Althing, dates from about 930 and is one of the oldest parliamentary institutions anywhere. Iceland accepted Christianity by a decision of that assembly around the year 1000, and produced the sagas two centuries later.

steps.name: The grant of Normandy
steps.page: In 911 the Frankish king Charles the Simple granted land around the lower Seine to a Norse leader the sources call Rollo, in return for his allegiance and for defending the river against other Northmen. The settlement kept its name, Normandy, the land of the Northmen, and lost its language and religion within two generations. Its dukes became one of the most formidable powers in France, and in 1066 one of them [took England](event:hastings).

steps.name: Greenland
steps.page: Erik the Red, outlawed from Iceland, led settlers to the south-western fjords of Greenland in about 985. Two settlements grew to perhaps two or three thousand people, living by stock-rearing, seal hunting and the export of walrus ivory, and holding a bishopric from 1126. They were the westernmost European communities in existence, and the base from which the Atlantic crossing was made.

steps.name: Cnut's North Sea empire
steps.page: The raiding of the late tenth century became conquest again: Sweyn Forkbeard took England in 1013, and his son Cnut ruled it from 1016 and Denmark from 1018, with Norway and part of Sweden added later. Cnut governed England as an English king, with English law, English coinage and the church's support, and went on pilgrimage to Rome. The empire fell apart at his death in 1035.

steps.name: Stamford Bridge and the end of the age
steps.page: Harald Hardrada of Norway, the last of the great Viking commanders, invaded England in September 1066 and was killed at Stamford Bridge by Harold Godwinson, who then marched south to meet [William of Normandy](event:hastings) at Hastings. The year is the conventional end of the age, though the deeper change was that Scandinavia had become Christian and had been organised into kingdoms whose rulers made war as European monarchs rather than as sea-captains.

name: Raid on Lindisfarne
summary: Norse raiders sacked the Northumbrian island monastery in 793, an event conventionally taken as the opening of the Viking Age in Europe.
body:
Part of [Viking Age](event:viking-age). On 8 June 793, raiders from Scandinavia attacked the monastery on Lindisfarne, a tidal island off the Northumbrian coast. They killed or carried off monks, took the church's treasure and left. The raid is conventionally treated as the opening of the Viking Age in western Europe, though smaller attacks on the English coast are recorded a few years earlier.

Lindisfarne was one of the most prestigious religious houses in Britain, founded by Irish monks from Iona in 635 and the home of St Cuthbert, whose shrine drew pilgrims and gifts. Like most monasteries it was rich, coastal and undefended. The *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* records the attack with portents, and the scholar Alcuin, then at Charlemagne's court, wrote letters asking how God could have permitted it.

The community stayed for another eighty years, then left in 875 carrying Cuthbert's body and the illuminated Lindisfarne Gospels, and settled eventually at Durham. Raids on the British and Irish coasts became annual within a generation, and by the 860s Danish armies were wintering in England rather than sailing home.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne).

name: Heian Period in Japan
summary: Four centuries of aristocratic court culture at Kyoto produced the Tale of Genji and Japan's own written literature, before power passed to the warriors.
body:
The Heian period ran from 794, when the imperial court moved to Heian-kyo (modern Kyoto), to 1185, when warrior government replaced it. Political power drifted from the emperor to the Fujiwara family, who governed as regents by marrying their daughters to emperors, and the court turned its attention to ceremony, poetry and aesthetics. It produced the first Japanese literature written in a Japanese script.

The court had stopped sending official embassies to Tang China by 894, and Chinese models were reworked into local forms. The *kana* syllabaries made it possible to write Japanese as it was spoken, and much of the best writing was done by women of the court, for whom Chinese was not the expected medium: Murasaki Shikibu's *Tale of Genji*, often called the world's first novel, and Sei Shonagon's *Pillow Book* both date from about 1000. Pure Land Buddhism spread beyond the aristocracy, promising rebirth in a paradise to anyone who called on Amida.

Outside the capital the tax system decayed as land passed into private estates, and provincial families kept armed retainers. Two of them, the Taira and the Minamoto, were drawn into court disputes and then fought each other; the Minamoto victory in 1185 opened the [Kamakura shogunate](event:kamakura-shogunate) and six centuries of rule by warriors.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heian_period).

name: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: The pope crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor in Rome on Christmas Day 800, reviving an imperial title in the west.
body:
On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor in St Peter's basilica in Rome. No one had held an imperial title in western Europe since 476. Charlemagne already ruled most of Latin Christendom. The title created a claim that European rulers contested for the next thousand years.

He had become sole king of the Franks in 771 and spent thirty years campaigning: against the Lombards in Italy, whose kingdom he annexed in 774; against the Saxons east of the Rhine, in a war of conquest and forced conversion lasting more than thirty years; against the Avars on the Danube; and across the Pyrenees, where his rearguard was destroyed at Roncesvalles. He governed through counts and travelling inspectors, and through bishops and abbots who were also royal officials.

His court at Aachen gathered scholars from across Europe, among them Alcuin of York, to correct church texts, standardise the liturgy and teach Latin, the revival of learning later called the Carolingian renaissance. Its clerks developed Carolingian minuscule, a clear script with word spacing and lower-case letters, in which most surviving classical Latin literature reaches us.

Byzantium, which regarded the title as its own, recognised his imperial rank only in 812. The empire was divided among his grandsons at Verdun in 843, along lines that sketch the later shape of France and Germany.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne).

name: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
summary: Al-Khwarizmi's treatise on balancing equations gave algebra its name, and the Latin form of his own name gave rise to "algorithm".
body:
Part of [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age). Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi was a scholar at the Abbasid court in Baghdad in the first half of the ninth century. His treatise on solving equations, *al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa-l-muqabala*, set out a systematic method for reducing problems to a small number of standard forms and solving them. The word *al-jabr*, the restoring of a subtracted term to the other side, became "algebra".

The book has no symbols in it. Everything is written out in words, with geometrical proofs for the rules, and the worked problems are the practical ones of inheritance shares, surveying and trade. What made it a new subject was the treatment: equations are objects to be manipulated by general rules, rather than puzzles each solved by its own trick.

He also wrote on the Indian decimal numerals, including zero and place value, and it was through a Latin translation of that work, beginning *Dixit Algorizmi*, that the system spread in Europe. His name in that form became "algorithm". He compiled astronomical tables and a revision of Ptolemy's geography as well.

Both books were translated in twelfth-century Spain and were standard European texts for centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi).

name: Invention of gunpowder
summary: Chinese alchemists found that a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal burns explosively; by the 13th century it was used in weapons.
body:
Gunpowder was discovered in China, probably in the ninth century, by alchemists mixing saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal in a search for medicines and an elixir of immortality. The earliest surviving written formulas appear in a Chinese military manual of 1044, which already gives several recipes and describes incendiary bombs.

Its military use developed over the following centuries. [Song](event:song-dynasty) armies used fire-lances, rockets and bombs against the Jin and later the Mongols; cast-iron bomb casings and the first hand cannon appear in the thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. The [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests) carried both the substance and the craftsmen across Eurasia, and gunpowder weapons are recorded in the Islamic world and in Europe by the 1280s and 1320s.

Early cannon were unreliable, but by the fifteenth century large siege guns could break masonry walls that had stood for centuries; Ottoman artillery took [Constantinople](event:fall-constantinople) in 1453. Fortification had to be redesigned around low, thick, angled earthworks. Handheld firearms took longer to displace the bow, but did so by the sixteenth century, and with them went the long training that had made a knight or an archer.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder).

name: Woodblock printing
summary: The Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868, is the oldest printed book that carries a date.
body:
Part of [Tang dynasty](event:tang-dynasty). Woodblock printing, which cuts a whole page in reverse into a block of wood, inks it and presses paper onto it, was in use in China by the seventh century. The oldest printed book bearing a date is a copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text, whose colophon records that it was made in 868 "for free general distribution" by a man named Wang Jie on behalf of his parents. It was found walled up in the Mogao caves at Dunhuang and is now in the British Library.

The technique suited Chinese writing. A page of several thousand distinct characters is no harder to cut as a block than a page of an alphabet, and a block once cut can be stored and reprinted for decades. Buddhist and Daoist texts, almanacs, dictionaries and charms were printed in quantity long before Europe printed anything, and the [Song](event:song-dynasty) state used the technique for law codes, examination texts and paper money.

Movable type was invented in China in the eleventh century and cast in metal [in Korea](event:korea-movable-type) by the thirteenth, but for long print runs in Chinese, blocks remained cheaper. The two technologies coexisted for centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodblock_printing).

name: Fatimid Caliphate
summary: A Shia caliphate ruling from Cairo controlled North Africa, Egypt and the Levant, and disputed religious authority with the Sunni Abbasids.
body:
The Fatimid caliphate was an Ismaili Shia dynasty that ruled North Africa from 909 and Egypt from 969, at its height controlling the Levant, the Hijaz with the holy cities, and Sicily. Its rulers claimed descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima and the title of caliph, in direct challenge to the Sunni Abbasids of Baghdad. For a time there were three rival caliphs in the Islamic world, the third at Córdoba.

The dynasty began among Berber converts in Ifriqiya, in present-day Tunisia, and moved east after conquering Egypt, where its general founded a new palace city, al-Qahira, now Cairo. The mosque and teaching college of al-Azhar, established there in 970, is still in use. Fatimid wealth came from Egyptian agriculture and from the Red Sea and Indian Ocean trade, which they redirected away from the Persian Gulf; Italian merchants dealt with them freely, and the trade survived the [Crusades](event:crusades).

Their religious mission had limited success: most Egyptians remained Sunni or Coptic Christian. Central authority weakened through the eleventh century under famine, army mutinies and rule by viziers rather than caliphs. [Saladin](event:saladin), sent to Egypt as a Syrian officer, ended the dynasty in 1171 and returned the country to Sunni allegiance.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatimid_Caliphate).

name: Song Dynasty
summary: A Chinese dynasty of dense cities, paper money, printing and landscape painting, which lost the north to the Jurchen and ruled from Hangzhou.
body:
The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279. It reunified the country after the collapse of the [Tang](event:tang-dynasty) but never recovered the northern frontier, and spent its whole existence dealing with powerful neighbours: the Liao, the Xia, the Jin and finally the [Mongols](event:mongol-conquests), usually by paying them. Inside those borders it was the wealthiest and most urbanised society in the world.

Agriculture came first: early-ripening rice from Champa allowed two harvests a year in the south, and the population roughly doubled to about 100 million. That surplus supported cities of a size Europe would not see for centuries, a national market linked by canals and coastal shipping, paid officials recruited by [examination](event:neo-confucianism) rather than birth, the world's first government-issued paper money, and iron production on a scale not matched until the industrial revolution. Compasses were used at sea, [gunpowder](event:gunpowder) weapons in war, and movable type was invented for printing.

The Jurchen took the capital Kaifeng in 1127 and with it the whole of northern China. The court re-established itself at Hangzhou as the Southern Song, turned toward maritime trade, and held out for another century and a half.

Painting, poetry and ceramics of this period are treated as classical in China, and [Neo-Confucian](event:neo-confucianism) philosophy became the orthodoxy of East Asia. Kublai Khan completed the conquest in 1279 and founded the [Yuan](event:yuan-dynasty).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_dynasty).

name: Avicenna and medieval medicine
summary: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine organised Greek, Persian and Indian medicine into one system and was a standard text for six centuries.
body:
Part of [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age). The *Canon of Medicine*, finished about 1025 by the Persian physician and philosopher [Ibn Sina](item:ibn-sina), known in Latin as Avicenna, gathered Greek, Persian, Indian and Arabic medical writing into a single ordered system. It runs to five books: general principles, a pharmacology of some 800 simple drugs, diseases by organ, diseases affecting the whole body, and compound remedies. It was the standard medical reference in both the Islamic world and Latin Europe for roughly six hundred years.

Earlier medicine existed as commentaries on Galen and Hippocrates and as collections of recipes; the *Canon* set out definitions, causes, symptoms and treatment in a fixed order that could be taught and examined. It insists that disease has natural causes, describes contagion, and lays down rules for testing whether a drug works: that it be tried on one condition at a time, that its effect be constant, and that trials on human beings settle the matter.

Translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona at Toledo in the twelfth century, it was printed more than thirty times before 1600 and taught in the medical faculties of Montpellier, Padua and Bologna into the seventeenth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canon_of_Medicine).

name: Ibn Sina
summary: Persian physician and philosopher, known in Europe as Avicenna, whose Canon of Medicine was a standard text for six centuries.
body:
Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), known in Latin Europe as Avicenna, was a Persian physician, philosopher and administrator. He is the central figure of philosophy in the Islamic world and the author of the [*Canon of Medicine*](event:avicenna), which was a standard medical text from Central Asia to Scotland for six hundred years.

He was born near Bukhara in the Samanid realm and was, by his own account, treating patients at sixteen and reading in the Samanid library soon after. The political disorder of the following decades left him moving between courts in Persia, among them Gurgan, Rayy, Hamadan and Isfahan, serving as court physician and sometimes as vizier, twice imprisoned, and writing at night and while travelling. Some 240 of his works survive.

The *Book of Healing*, his philosophical encyclopedia, covers logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics. Its central argument distinguishes what merely happens to exist from what must exist of itself, and it was taken up by Islamic, Jewish and Christian thinkers alike; Aquinas argues both with it and from it. He also wrote on the formation of mountains, on the psychology of the intellect, and on music.

His medicine was less original than his organisation of it: he made a teachable system out of Greek, Indian and Arabic material. He died at Hamadan in 1037. His works are among the main routes by which Greek learning re-entered Latin Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna).

name: Neo-Confucianism in Song China
summary: Song philosophers rebuilt Confucian ethics on a metaphysics borrowed from Buddhism and Daoism, creating the orthodoxy of East Asia.
body:
Part of [Song Dynasty](event:song-dynasty). Neo-Confucianism is the reworking of Confucian thought carried out by Chinese philosophers between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries. Confucianism had always been strong on ethics and government and weak on questions of cosmology and mind, which is where Buddhism and Daoism had drawn adherents for centuries. The Song thinkers answered those questions in Confucian terms, and the result became the state orthodoxy of China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for most of the next seven hundred years.

Its central concepts are *li*, the pattern or principle underlying everything, and *qi*, the material force in which that pattern is realised. Human nature is *li* and is therefore good; wrongdoing comes from turbid *qi*, and self-cultivation is the work of clearing it, through study, ritual and what the school called the investigation of things.

Zhu Xi (1130–1200) synthesised the work of his predecessors and selected four short texts as the core curriculum: the *Analects*, the *Mencius*, the *Great Learning* and the *Doctrine of the Mean*. From 1313 his commentaries on them were the set answer in the imperial examinations, which made his reading of Confucius the definition of an educated person in East Asia until the twentieth century.

The [Song](event:song-dynasty) state, printing and the examination system spread it; later critics inside the tradition, notably Wang Yangming, disputed its emphasis on external study.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Confucianism).

name: Chimú Empire
summary: The Chimú built the largest state on the Peruvian coast before the Inca, ruling from the adobe city of Chan Chan.
body:
Chimor, the kingdom of the Chimú, was the largest state on the Peruvian coast before the Inca. From about 900 it grew out of the Moche valley until it controlled roughly a thousand kilometres of desert coastline, watered by an irrigation system that carried river water between valleys. The Inca conquered it around 1470.

Its capital, Chan Chan, near modern Trujillo, is the largest adobe city in the Americas: about twenty square kilometres, of which the core is a set of nine or ten walled compounds. Each appears to have belonged to one ruler, who was buried in it, after which his successor built another. Under this arrangement of split inheritance each new king had to acquire fresh territory and revenue.

Chimú craftsmen worked gold, silver and copper alloys, hammered and joined rather than cast, and produced textiles and blackware ceramics in quantity through what was effectively workshop production.

When the Inca took the kingdom they moved its metalworkers to Cuzco and absorbed its road system, its administrative methods and much of its aesthetic. Spanish looting of Chan Chan began in the 1530s and continued for centuries; the site is now a UNESCO World Heritage site threatened by rain that its builders' climate rarely delivered.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimor).

name: Norse reach North America
summary: Norse settlers from Greenland built a small camp at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland around 1000, five centuries before Columbus.
body:
Part of [Viking Age](event:viking-age). Around the year 1000, Norse voyagers from the Greenland colony crossed to the north-east coast of North America and built a settlement at what is now L'Anse aux Meadows, at the northern tip of Newfoundland. It is the only confirmed Norse site in the Americas, and the earliest known European presence there, about five centuries before [Columbus](event:columbus).

The Icelandic sagas, written down two centuries later, describe voyages by Leif Erikson and others to lands they called Helluland, Markland and Vinland, and conflict with people they called *skraelings*. The site was found in 1960 by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad and excavated over the following decade: eight turf buildings, a smithy with iron slag, and objects including a bronze cloak pin and a soapstone spindle whorl. Wood from the site was cut in 1021, a date fixed by the ring signature of a known solar storm.

It was a base rather than a colony, perhaps a repair and staging camp for expeditions further south, used by a few dozen people for a few years. Timber and butternuts found there come from further south, so the Norse ranged beyond it. The Greenland colonies themselves lasted until the fifteenth century, and were abandoned as the climate cooled in the [Little Ice Age](event:little-ice-age).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_colonization_of_North_America).

name: Seljuk Empire
summary: Turkic nomads from Central Asia took Persia, Iraq and Anatolia, ruled as patrons of Persian culture, and provoked the Crusades.
body:
The Seljuks were a Turkic clan from the Central Asian steppe who converted to Sunni Islam and, in the middle of the eleventh century, took over most of the Islamic east. Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055 and was named sultan by the Abbasid caliph, who kept religious authority while the Seljuks held the armies and the revenue. At their height they ruled from western Anatolia to the borders of India.

They governed through Persian bureaucrats and in the Persian language. The vizier Nizam al-Mulk, who served two sultans for thirty years, wrote a manual of government still read as a classic and founded a network of state-funded colleges, the *nizamiyya*, to train officials and defend Sunni orthodoxy; [al-Ghazali](event:al-ghazali) taught at the one in Baghdad.

Their victory over the Byzantine emperor at [Manzikert](event:manzikert) in 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement, and the appeal Byzantium sent west for help was one of the immediate causes of the [First Crusade](event:first-crusade).

The empire divided among rival princes after 1092 and had broken into successor states well before the Mongols arrived. One of them, the Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia, outlasted the rest; from its fragments the [Ottomans](event:ottoman-empire) later emerged.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seljuk_Empire).

name: Cahokia mound city
summary: The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico stood near modern St Louis, and was abandoned by about 1350.
body:
Cahokia was a Mississippian city on the Mississippi floodplain opposite present-day St Louis. Between about 1050 and 1350 it was the largest settlement north of Mexico, with a population usually estimated at 10,000 to 20,000, comparable to London at the same date, and it was the centre of a culture whose goods and religious symbols spread across the eastern woodlands.

Its people built earthen mounds: at least 120 at the site, of which Monks Mound is the largest earthwork in the Americas, about 30 metres high on a base larger than that of the Great Pyramid. Around it stood a plaza, ranks of smaller platform and burial mounds, thousands of houses, and a circle of posts used to track the sun. Building it took an estimated fifteen million baskets of earth. Mound 72 held a burial accompanied by more than 250 other bodies, many of them apparently sacrificed.

The city grew quickly around 1050, an expansion the archaeological literature calls the "big bang", and was abandoned over the following three centuries. No single explanation is accepted: drought recorded in tree rings, flooding, deforestation and depletion of firewood and game, and political or religious breakdown have all been proposed, and a defensive palisade rebuilt several times suggests conflict. The site was empty long before Europeans reached the valley.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahokia).

name: East–West Schism
summary: Mutual excommunications in 1054 between Rome and Constantinople marked the split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
body:
In July 1054 a papal legation in Constantinople laid a bull of excommunication against the patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch's synod excommunicated the legates in return. The exchange is the conventional date of the East–West Schism, the division between the Catholic and Orthodox churches that has lasted since.

The estrangement was much older than the event. Latin and Greek Christianity had drifted apart in language, liturgy and law for centuries, and disputed two substantial questions: whether the pope held authority over the whole church or a primacy of honour among patriarchs, and whether the Latin addition of *filioque*, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father "and the Son", could be inserted into the creed without a council. Practical quarrels over unleavened bread, clerical marriage and jurisdiction in southern Italy sharpened both.

Contemporaries did not treat 1054 as a final rupture; the excommunications were personal, not directed at the churches as such, and relations continued. What made the break permanent was the [Fourth Crusade](event:fourth-crusade)'s sack of Constantinople in 1204, after which reunion councils at Lyon in 1274 and Florence in 1439 were rejected by the Orthodox faithful.

The excommunications of 1054 were finally withdrawn by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras in 1965. The churches remain separate.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Schism).

name: Al-Ghazali and Islamic theology
summary: The Persian theologian attacked the metaphysics of the philosophers while making Sufism respectable.
body:
Part of [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age). Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111) was a Persian jurist, theologian and mystic, and one of the most influential figures in Sunni Islam. He held the senior chair at the Nizamiyya college in Baghdad in his thirties, abandoned it in 1095 in a personal crisis, spent about a decade travelling and living as an ascetic, and then returned to teaching.

He learned philosophy in order to refute it. His *Aims of the Philosophers* summarises the system of [Ibn Sina](item:ibn-sina) so accurately that Latin readers took it for his own view, and his *Incoherence of the Philosophers* then attacks it on twenty points, among them the claims that the world is eternal, that God knows only universals, and that there is no bodily resurrection. His argument that what we call causation is observed regularity rather than necessity anticipates a line later associated with Hume. Ibn Rushd replied at length in the *Incoherence of the Incoherence*.

His largest work, the *Revival of the Religious Sciences*, sets law, theology and Sufi practice side by side and argues that ritual observance without inward discipline is empty. It did much to make Sufism a respectable part of mainstream Sunni religion.

The autobiographical *Deliverance from Error*, describing his loss of confidence in every kind of authority and his recovery through direct experience, is a classic of the genre.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ghazali).

name: Norman conquest of England
summary: William of Normandy defeated King Harold at Hastings in October 1066 and took the English throne, replacing the country's ruling class.
body:
On 14 October 1066, William, duke of Normandy, defeated and killed the English king Harold Godwinson at a ridge near Hastings on the Sussex coast. He was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day, and spent the next five years suppressing revolts. The conquest replaced England's aristocracy and church leadership almost entirely, and reoriented the kingdom toward France for four hundred years.

Edward the Confessor had died childless in January 1066, and three men claimed the succession: Harold, the most powerful English earl, who was crowned at once; William, who said Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to support him; and the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada. Harold destroyed Hardrada's army at Stamford Bridge in Yorkshire on 25 September, then marched south. At Hastings his infantry shield wall held most of the day against Norman cavalry and archers before breaking.

Resistance in the north was ended by the "harrying" of 1069–70, in which William's troops laid waste large areas of Yorkshire. Land was redistributed to a few thousand Norman and French followers, castles were built to hold the country, and by the time of the [Domesday survey](event:domesday-book) in 1086 almost no major English landholder remained.

French became the language of the court and the law for three centuries, and left several thousand words in English. The Norman kings' continental possessions bound England to French politics down to the [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest).

name: Battle of Manzikert
summary: A Seljuk victory in 1071 destroyed the Byzantine field army and opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.
body:
At Manzikert, in what is now eastern Turkey, on 26 August 1071, the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated a Byzantine army and captured the emperor Romanos IV Diogenes. The defeat itself cost the empire little territory, since Alp Arslan released the emperor on terms, but the civil war that followed in Constantinople left Anatolia undefended, and Turkish groups moved into it within a decade.

Byzantium had held the Anatolian plateau for centuries; it supplied most of the empire's soldiers, horses and grain. The army Romanos led east was large but made up of mercenaries and provincial levies of uneven quality, and part of it withdrew from the field rather than fight. He was deposed and blinded on his return, and rival claimants spent the following years fighting each other, some of them hiring Turkish troops.

By 1080 Turkish rulers held Nicaea, within sight of Constantinople across the water. The empire's appeal to the Latin west for mercenaries was one of the immediate reasons Pope Urban II preached the [First Crusade](event:first-crusade) in 1095.

The loss of Anatolia was permanent in the long run: it removed the empire's recruiting ground, and the settlement that followed began the process by which the peninsula became Turkish and Muslim, completed under the [Ottomans](event:ottoman-empire).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Manzikert).

name: Domesday Book
summary: William I's survey of England in 1086 recorded who held what land, and what it was worth, village by village.
body:
Part of [Norman conquest of England](event:hastings). The Domesday Book is the record of a survey of England ordered by William the Conqueror at Christmas 1085 and carried out during 1086. Royal commissioners went circuit by circuit, taking sworn evidence from juries of local men in every shire and hundred, and recorded who had held each estate before the conquest, who held it now, how many ploughs, tenants, mills and animals it had, and what it was worth. It covers about 13,000 places.

Nothing on this scale had been attempted in medieval Europe, and its purpose was practical: William had given England away to his followers and needed to know what he and they actually held, and what could be taxed. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle complains that not one hide, ox, cow or pig was left out.

The name came later and was not affectionate: its verdicts were final, like those of the Last Judgement, and there was no appeal. It survives in two volumes, Great and Little Domesday, and remained admissible evidence of tenure in English courts into the twentieth century.

For historians it is the most detailed picture of any eleventh-century society in Europe: it shows the scale of land transfer after [1066](event:hastings), with almost all major estates in Norman hands, and the extent of slavery and depopulation in parts of the country.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domesday_Book).

name: First universities
summary: Bologna, then Paris and Oxford, organised teachers and students into self-governing corporations that awarded degrees.
body:
The university as an institution began in Europe around 1100. Bologna, conventionally dated to 1088, grew out of schools of Roman law; Paris out of the cathedral schools, and Oxford from about 1167. What was new was not teaching but the corporation: masters and students organised themselves as a guild, a *universitas*, which set its own curriculum, examined candidates, granted a licence to teach anywhere, and could bargain with town and church by threatening to leave.

At Bologna the students formed the guild and hired the professors; at Paris the masters did, which is the model most later universities followed. Both won charters of privilege that removed their members from the ordinary jurisdiction of the town.

The curriculum began with the seven liberal arts and went on to the higher faculties of law, medicine and theology. Its raw material was the newly available Latin translations of Aristotle and of Arabic commentary and science, and the method was disputation: a question put, arguments assembled on both sides, and a resolution reasoned out. That is the setting in which [scholasticism](event:scholasticism) developed.

Perhaps eighty universities existed in Europe by 1500. The degrees, the faculties, the lecture and the examination all descend from these foundations.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna).

name: The Crusades
summary: Two centuries of religious warfare launched from Latin Europe against the Muslim states of the eastern Mediterranean.
body:
The Crusades were a series of wars called by the papacy, fought mainly between 1095 and 1291, in which armies from Latin Europe attacked Muslim states in the eastern Mediterranean and held territory there. Those who took the cross were promised remission of the penalties of sin. Four Crusader states were established in the Levant after the first expedition; the last of them was lost in 1291.

The immediate occasion was a Byzantine appeal for troops after [Manzikert](event:manzikert). Behind it lay a papacy asserting leadership over Latin Christendom, a warrior aristocracy with more sons than land, and an established practice of armed pilgrimage. Pope Urban II preached the first expedition at Clermont in 1095; the response was far larger than he had asked for.

Only the first campaign achieved its stated aim. Later expeditions were beaten, diverted or negotiated away, and the [Fourth](event:fourth-crusade) sacked Christian Constantinople instead. Crusades were also preached elsewhere: against the Muslims of [Iberia](event:reconquista), against pagans on the Baltic, and against heretics in southern France. The model outlasted the Levantine wars by centuries.

The consequences were mixed and are still argued over. Trade with the Levant grew and Italian ports profited; Arabic science and Greek texts came west through Spain and Sicily more than through Syria; Jewish communities in the Rhineland were massacred by armies on their way east; and the sack of Constantinople left Byzantium permanently weakened. In the Muslim world the wars were a frontier problem rather than a defining event, and were given their modern symbolic weight only in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

The numbered expeditions are listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades).

steps.name: Urban II preaches at Clermont
steps.page: At the council of Clermont on 27 November 1095, Pope Urban II called on the knighthood of France to march east, to help the eastern Christians and to recover Jerusalem, and offered remission of penance to those who went. Preachers carried the appeal far beyond the intended audience, and poorly organised popular bands set out ahead of the armies, attacking Jewish communities in the Rhineland on the way; most were destroyed in Anatolia.

steps.name: The Crusader states
steps.page: Four Latin states were left behind by the first expedition: the kingdom of Jerusalem, the county of Tripoli, the principality of Antioch and the county of Edessa. They were small, dependent on a stream of pilgrims and reinforcements, and held together by castles and by the [military orders](event:knights-templar). Their neighbours were divided, which is much of why they survived at all.

steps.name: Second Crusade
steps.page: The loss of Edessa in 1144 brought a second expedition, preached by Bernard of Clairvaux and led by the kings of France and Germany. Both armies were badly mauled crossing Anatolia, and the attack they made on Damascus, a city then friendly to Jerusalem, collapsed after four days. The failure damaged the standing of crusading in Europe for a generation.

steps.name: Third Crusade
steps.page: The emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II of France and Richard I of England went east in response. Frederick drowned on the way, Philip went home after the fall of Acre, and Richard beat Saladin at Arsuf and twice came within reach of Jerusalem without attacking it. The truce of 1192 left the Latins a coastal strip and pilgrims the right of access to the city.

steps.name: The Egyptian crusades
steps.page: Later strategy aimed at Egypt, the base of Ayyubid power. The Fifth Crusade took Damietta in 1219 and lost it in 1221 when the Nile flooded around its army. Frederick II recovered Jerusalem by treaty in 1229 without fighting, and the city was lost again in 1244. Louis IX of France repeated the Damietta plan in 1249, was defeated at Mansurah and captured, and was ransomed in 1250.

name: First Crusade
summary: A Latin army crossed Anatolia and took Jerusalem in July 1099, massacring much of the population and founding four Crusader states.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). The First Crusade was the expedition called by Pope Urban II in 1095. Armies from France, Germany, southern Italy and Flanders assembled at Constantinople in 1096–97, crossed Anatolia, took Antioch after an eight-month siege, and captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099. It was the only crusade to achieve what it set out to do.

The march was disastrous for those who made it. Of perhaps 60,000 who set out, a minority reached Jerusalem; the rest died of hunger, thirst and disease, turned back, or stayed in the territories taken on the way. At Antioch the besiegers were themselves besieged and were held together partly by the discovery of a relic said to be the Holy Lance. The lack of a single commander was managed by a council of princes and constant argument.

Jerusalem was defended by an Egyptian garrison and fell after a five-week siege and an assault from siege towers. The sack that followed killed most of the city's Muslim and Jewish inhabitants; the Latin and Arabic accounts differ on numbers but not on the fact.

Four states were founded, at Jerusalem, Antioch, Tripoli and Edessa, and held for varying lengths of time up to the fall of [Acre](event:acre-1291) in 1291. The massacre at Jerusalem is remembered in Muslim historiography as the defining act of the [Crusades](event:crusades).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade).

name: Great Zimbabwe
summary: A Shona city in south-east Africa built mortarless stone enclosures and grew rich on the gold trade with the Indian Ocean coast.
body:
Great Zimbabwe was a city in the granite uplands of what is now southern Zimbabwe, occupied from about 1100 and at its height in the fourteenth century, when it may have held 10,000 to 18,000 people. Its rulers controlled the routes by which gold and ivory from the interior reached Swahili ports on the Indian Ocean, and through them Arabia, India and China. It gave the modern country its name.

Its builders, ancestors of the Shona, cut granite into blocks and laid them without mortar into curving walls up to eleven metres high and five metres thick. The Great Enclosure, the largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa, encloses a conical tower whose purpose is unknown. Finds at the site include Persian and Chinese ceramics, Arab coins and eight carved soapstone birds, one of which appears on Zimbabwe's flag.

European visitors from the sixteenth century onward, and the Rhodesian government well into the twentieth, attributed the ruins to Phoenicians, Arabs or the Queen of Sheba, and the colonial administration suppressed archaeological conclusions to the contrary. African construction has not been in serious doubt among archaeologists since the 1930s.

The city declined in the fifteenth century. Exhausted soil and pasture, the shifting of the gold trade north toward the Zambezi, and political fragmentation have all been proposed; successor states, Mutapa and Torwa, took over its trade.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe).

name: Venetian–Genoese rivalry
summary: Two Italian maritime republics fought four wars over the trade of the Mediterranean and Black Sea, and developed the tools of modern commerce.
body:
Venice and Genoa were the dominant maritime republics of the medieval Mediterranean, and between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries they were commercial rivals and periodic enemies. Both lived by carrying eastern goods, among them spices, silk, alum, grain and slaves, to European markets, and both wanted the same harbours, quarters and privileges in Constantinople, the Levant and the Black Sea.

They fought four wars, in 1256–70, 1294–99, 1350–55 and 1377–81. Genoa gained most after the [Fourth Crusade's](event:fourth-crusade) Latin regime in Constantinople collapsed in 1261, and its colonies at Pera and Kaffa in the Crimea gave it the Black Sea trade, the route by which the [Black Death](event:black-death) reached Europe. The last war, fought largely in the Venetian lagoon at Chioggia, ended with Genoa checked and Venice dominant for the next century.

To finance and insure voyages the two cities developed instruments that became standard European practice: the commenda partnership, the bill of exchange, marine insurance, public debt in transferable shares, and double-entry bookkeeping, first described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494. Genoese capital and Genoese navigators, [Columbus](event:columbus) among them, later moved into the service of Iberian crowns.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venetian%E2%80%93Genoese_wars).

name: Angkor Wat built
summary: The Khmer king Suryavarman II built the largest religious monument in the world, first Hindu and later Buddhist.
body:
Angkor Wat was built in the first half of the twelfth century by the Khmer king Suryavarman II, as a temple to Vishnu and as his own funerary monument. Its outer wall encloses about 160 hectares, which makes it the largest religious structure in the world. It stands at Angkor, the capital of the Khmer empire, on the plain north of the Tonle Sap in present-day Cambodia.

The plan is a model of the Hindu cosmos: five towers in the form of lotus buds representing the peaks of Mount Meru, three rising galleries, and a moat 190 metres wide standing for the surrounding ocean. Unusually among Khmer temples it faces west. Nearly 600 metres of bas-relief run around the third gallery, showing scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, a procession of Suryavarman's army, and the churning of the sea of milk. The sandstone was floated from a quarry some 40 kilometres away along canals.

The empire around it depended on an immense system of reservoirs and channels that stored monsoon water for the dry season, supporting one of the largest pre-industrial urban complexes known.

The temple was converted to Theravada Buddhist use in the later Middle Ages and, unlike most of Angkor, was never abandoned. It appears on Cambodia's flag.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat).

name: Knights Templar
summary: A military-monastic order founded to protect pilgrims to Jerusalem became a landholder and banker across Christendom, and was suppressed in 1312.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon were founded about 1119 in the kingdom of Jerusalem to protect pilgrims on the roads from the coast. They were the first of the military orders: monks under vows who also fought. Endorsed by the Church in 1129 and promoted by Bernard of Clairvaux, they attracted donations across Europe and became one of the wealthiest institutions in Christendom.

Their fighting strength was small, a few hundred knights in the east at any time, supported by sergeants and hired troops, but they were disciplined and permanently in the field, and they garrisoned the [Crusader states'](event:crusades) key castles. Their reputation suffered badly after the defeat at Hattin in 1187, where the order's leadership pressed for the battle and its captured brothers were executed.

The estates given to support that effort made them bankers. A pilgrim could deposit money in Paris or London and draw it in Acre; the order lent to kings, held royal treasuries, and answered to the pope alone.

After [Acre](event:acre-1291) fell in 1291 they had no front to hold. Philip IV of France, in debt to them and short of money, had every Templar in France arrested on 13 October 1307 and charged with heresy, blasphemy and sodomy; confessions were obtained under torture and later retracted. Pope Clement V dissolved the order in 1312, and the last grand master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in Paris in 1314.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_Templar).

name: Zagwe dynasty in Ethiopia
summary: After Aksum's decline, Christian rule shifted to the Ethiopian highlands under the Zagwe kings, who cut the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela.
body:
The Zagwe were a Christian dynasty that ruled the northern Ethiopian highlands from about 1137 to 1270, in the long gap between the collapse of the kingdom of Aksum and the rise of the Solomonic line. Their power was centred on Lasta, south of the old Aksumite heartland, and they are remembered above all for the rock-hewn churches at Lalibela.

The name comes from Ze-Agaw, "of the Agaw", the people the dynasty came from. Aksum had lost its Red Sea outlets and its trade centuries earlier and Ethiopian Christianity had drawn back into the interior; the Zagwe inherited that inland kingdom and held the highlands of what is now Eritrea, Tigray, Wag and Bete Amhara, and westward toward Lake Tana. The church remained tied to the Coptic patriarch in Alexandria, who appointed its head, and Ethiopian monks and pilgrims are recorded in Egypt and Jerusalem in this period.

King Gebre Meskel Lalibela, who reigned in the early thirteenth century, gave his name to the eleven churches cut down into the living rock at his capital, which he laid out with the names and features of Jerusalem. They are still in use.

In 1270 Yekuno Amlak defeated and killed the last Zagwe king and founded the Solomonic dynasty, which claimed descent from Solomon and the queen of Sheba and ruled Ethiopia until 1974.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zagwe_dynasty).

name: Genghis Khan
summary: Mongol ruler who united the steppe tribes and founded the largest contiguous land empire in history.
body:
Born Temüjin, the son of a minor chieftain poisoned when the boy was nine, he grew up in poverty and captivity on the eastern steppe. Through alliance, patronage and a series of steppe wars he united the Mongol and Turkic tribes, and in 1206 an assembly [proclaimed him Genghis Khan](item:genghis-khan), universal ruler.

He reorganised his followers into decimal units that cut across tribal loyalties, promoted officers on merit, adopted a written script for the Mongol language and issued a body of law, the *yassa*. The armies that resulted took northern China, Central Asia and Persia within two decades; the [campaigns](item:mongol-conquests) were highly destructive, and the sack of cities that resisted was policy rather than accident.

The empire he left reached from Korea to the Caspian and, under his successors, from Hungary to the Pacific. Mongol control of the [trade routes across Eurasia](item:silk-roads) moved goods, techniques and, in all likelihood, the plague that became the [Black Death](item:black-death). His burial place is unknown.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan).

name: Saladin and the crusader wars
summary: The Kurdish general united much of the Islamic world against the crusaders, retook Jerusalem and founded the Ayyubid dynasty.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, called Saladin in European usage, was a Kurdish soldier who made himself ruler of Egypt and Syria, destroyed the field army of the kingdom of Jerusalem at Hattin in 1187, and recovered the city for Islam after eighty-eight years of Latin rule. He founded the Ayyubid dynasty, and is one of the few figures of the period celebrated in Muslim and European tradition alike.

He came to Egypt in 1169 as a junior officer on a Syrian expedition sent by Nur al-Din, became vizier, and in 1171 ended the Shia [Fatimid caliphate](event:fatimid-caliphate), returning the country to Sunni allegiance. After Nur al-Din's death in 1174 he spent a decade taking Damascus, Aleppo and Mosul from his old master's heirs, which for the first time put the crusader states between two halves of one state.

On 4 July 1187 he destroyed the army of Jerusalem at the Horns of Hattin, above Tiberias, having drawn it away from water in high summer. Most of the kingdom's towns and castles surrendered within months, and Jerusalem itself capitulated on terms in October; the inhabitants were ransomed rather than massacred, in deliberate contrast to 1099.

The Third Crusade recovered the coastal towns but not the city. Saladin agreed a truce with Richard I in 1192 that guaranteed Christian pilgrims access to Jerusalem, and died at Damascus the following year, having given away so much that his estate could not pay for his funeral.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saladin).

name: Kamakura shogunate
summary: Military rule by the shoguns began in Japan; the samurai became the ruling class and Zen Buddhism took root.
body:
The Kamakura shogunate was the first of Japan's warrior governments. Minamoto no Yoritomo, victor in the Genpei War, took the title of shogun in 1192 and ruled from Kamakura, several hundred kilometres east of the imperial court at Kyoto, which kept its ceremonial authority and lost its power. Warriors governed Japan on this pattern for the next seven centuries.

Yoritomo's authority rested on personal bonds with his vassals, whom he appointed as military governors of provinces and as stewards on estates, a structure that inserted warriors into the landholding of the old [Heian](event:heian-period) order rather than replacing it.
