His own line died out within a generation, and real power passed to the Hojo family, who ruled as regents for figurehead shoguns.

Mongol fleets sent by Kublai Khan attacked Kyushu in 1274 and again in 1281, in the largest seaborne invasions attempted anywhere before the twentieth century. Both were beaten off with the help of storms that later tradition called *kamikaze*, divine winds. Victory brought no conquered land to distribute, and the cost of the coastal defences and of rewarding the defenders strained the shogunate badly.

The period was also one of religious change. Zen arrived from China and found patrons among the warriors, while Pure Land and Nichiren preachers carried Buddhism to people the old monastic schools had never reached. Emperor Go-Daigo, backed by disaffected warriors including Ashikaga Takauji, overthrew the Hojo in 1333.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamakura_shogunate).

name: Decline of the Khmer Empire
summary: The Khmer empire that built Angkor gradually abandoned it, amid drought, war with Ayutthaya and a shift of power downriver.
body:
Part of [Angkor Wat built](event:angkor-wat). Between the thirteenth and the fifteenth centuries the Khmer empire lost the capital that had defined it. Angkor was not sacked and abandoned in a single event: the court's centre of gravity moved south-east toward Phnom Penh over several generations, and the great temples stayed in use throughout.

Angkor was the largest low-density urban complex known from the pre-industrial world, and it depended on an engineered landscape of reservoirs, canals and embankments that held monsoon water for the dry season. Tree-ring records from the region show two prolonged droughts, in the mid-fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries, broken by unusually heavy monsoons; excavation shows canals cut through, silted and never repaired. A system that had taken centuries to build could not be maintained once it began to fail in several places at once.

Other pressures ran alongside. The turn from the Hindu and Mahayana royal cults to Theravada Buddhism, which had no use for temple-building on the old scale, removed much of the reason for enormous royal foundations. Trade was shifting to maritime routes and to river ports better placed to serve them. And the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya was expanding: it took Angkor in 1431, the date usually given for the end.

The court settled near Phnom Penh. Monks went on maintaining [Angkor Wat](event:angkor-wat) itself, which was never abandoned, and the European travellers who reached it from the sixteenth century onward found it occupied.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_Empire).

name: Scholasticism peaks
summary: Medieval university philosophers used logic to reconcile faith and reason, culminating in the systems of Aquinas and Duns Scotus.
body:
Scholasticism was the method of teaching and argument developed in the medieval [universities](event:university-bologna) of western Europe, at its height in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its subject was the relation between Christian doctrine and reason, and above all the philosophy of Aristotle, whose complete works reached Latin readers in the twelfth century through translations from Arabic and Greek.

The method was as characteristic as the doctrine. A question was posed; the authorities on each side were assembled; the objections were stated in their strongest form; a resolution was reasoned out, and each objection answered in turn. Peter Abelard's *Sic et Non* had set the problem out by listing contradictory passages from the Fathers without resolving any of them, and Peter Lombard's *Sentences* became the textbook that every master had to lecture on.

Its best-known figure is Thomas Aquinas, whose *Summa Theologiae* argued that faith and reason cannot finally conflict because both come from God. Albertus Magnus taught him; Bonaventure argued from an Augustinian position against the Aristotelians; Duns Scotus and later William of Ockham disputed how far unaided reason could reach at all, and Ockham's refusal to multiply entities without necessity became a general principle of later thought.

Humanists of the [Renaissance](event:renaissance) mocked scholastic Latin and scholastic questions, and the natural philosophers of the seventeenth century defined themselves against both. The lecture, the commentary, the disputation and the formal defence of a thesis remained in use in European universities.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholasticism).

name: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
summary: Diverted by Venetian debts and dynastic politics, the crusaders stormed and looted Constantinople, the largest Christian city in the world.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). The Fourth Crusade was called by Pope Innocent III in 1198 and was meant to attack Egypt. It never reached the Levant. In April 1204 its army stormed Constantinople, the largest and richest Christian city in the world, sacked it for three days and installed a Latin emperor in place of the Byzantine one.

The diversion began as a debt. The crusaders had contracted with Venice for a fleet sized for an army far larger than the one that assembled, and could not pay for it. Venice proposed that they work the debt off by recovering the Adriatic port of Zara, a Christian city under Hungarian protection; they took it in 1202 and were excommunicated for it. At Zara they were joined by Alexios Angelos, son of a deposed Byzantine emperor, who promised money, troops and the submission of the Greek church in return for being placed on the throne. He was placed on it, could not pay either, and was killed in a coup, after which the army outside decided to take the city for itself.

The plunder was thorough, and included the relics, libraries and bronzes of a thousand years; the four horses on the front of St Mark's in Venice were carried off then. The Latin empire that followed lasted until 1261 and left Byzantium permanently reduced, which made the [Ottoman conquest](event:fall-constantinople) of 1453 far easier. Innocent III condemned the sack once he heard what had happened. The breach between the Greek and Latin churches never healed after it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade).

name: Mongol conquests
summary: The largest contiguous land empire in history was assembled in three generations, from Korea to Hungary.
body:
The Mongol conquests were the campaigns by which Genghis Khan and his descendants assembled the largest contiguous land empire in history, reaching from Korea to the Danube and from Siberia to the Persian Gulf. They ran from the [proclamation of Genghis Khan](event:genghis-khan) in 1206 to the death of his grandson Kublai in 1294, by which time the empire had already broken into four rival khanates.

Mongol forces were usually smaller than those they faced, but were composed almost entirely of mounted archers who could move at a pace their enemies could not match, were organised in decimal units that cut across tribal loyalty, and were held to an unusually harsh discipline. They learned siege warfare from Chinese and Muslim engineers taken into their service, which is what allowed steppe cavalry to reduce walled cities. Terror was used deliberately: a city that resisted after being summoned to surrender could expect to be destroyed and its people killed, and word of that made the next city surrender.

The destruction was real and in places demographic. The irrigation works of Persia and the cities of Khwarazm did not recover for centuries, and the [sack of Baghdad](event:baghdad-1258) in 1258 ended five centuries of Abbasid caliphate. The figures the chroniclers give for the dead are not credible as arithmetic, and modern estimates are much lower.

One authority from the Black Sea to the Pacific then made the overland routes safe enough that merchants, envoys, missionaries and craftsmen crossed Eurasia in numbers, [Marco Polo](event:marco-polo) among them, carrying goods, techniques and, in all likelihood, the plague that became the [Black Death](event:black-death). Chinese gunpowder and printing, Persian astronomy and Islamic medicine all travelled the same roads.

The empire could not hold itself together. Succession was decided by assembly and every one of them was contested; after the civil war of 1260–64 the four khanates, the [Yuan](event:yuan-dynasty) in China, the Chagatai in Central Asia, the Ilkhanate in Persia and the Golden Horde on the steppe, went their own ways, adopted the religions and the administrations of the people they ruled, and fought each other.

The campaigns are listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_conquests).

steps.name: Western Xia and the Jin
steps.page: The first campaigns were against the two states on the Mongols' southern border. The Tangut kingdom of Western Xia was raided from 1209 and destroyed in 1227. The Jin empire of northern China was attacked from 1211; its capital Zhongdu, on the site of modern Beijing, fell in 1215 after a siege and was burnt. The Jin held out south of the Yellow River until 1234. These wars gave the Mongols engineers, siege equipment and administrators.

steps.name: The Khwarazmian campaign
steps.page: The shah of Khwarazm had a Mongol trade caravan killed and then executed the envoys sent to complain. The response destroyed his empire in two years. Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv and Nishapur were taken and their populations killed or enslaved; the shah died a fugitive on an island in the Caspian. A detachment under Jebe and Subutai rode on round the Caspian, beat a Rus' and Cuman army at the Kalka river in 1223, and returned by way of the steppe.

steps.name: The death of Genghis Khan
steps.page: Genghis Khan died in August 1227, campaigning again against Western Xia. His burial place was deliberately concealed and has never been found. The empire passed, after two years of regency, to his third son Ögedei, who was elected at a *kurultai* in 1229 and built a capital at Karakorum. Succession by assembly rather than by rule was the flaw that eventually broke the empire apart.

steps.name: The western campaign
steps.page: An army under Batu, Genghis's grandson, with Subutai directing the operations, crossed the Volga in 1236. Volga Bulgaria, Ryazan, Vladimir and finally Kiev in December 1240 were taken and destroyed; the Rus' principalities became tributaries of what became the Golden Horde. In 1241 two Mongol forces beat a Polish and German army at Legnica and the Hungarian army at Mohi within two days of each other. They withdrew from central Europe in 1242, after news arrived that Ögedei had died.

steps.name: Checked at Ain Jalut
steps.page: On 3 September 1260, at Ain Jalut in Galilee, a Mamluk army from Egypt destroyed a Mongol force that Hulagu had left behind when he withdrew east with the bulk of his troops. It was the first strategic defeat the Mongols had suffered, and it fixed the western limit of their expansion at the Euphrates. The Mamluk sultanate that won it went on to take the last of the crusader states.

steps.name: The conquest of Song China
steps.page: The Southern Song were the hardest of the Mongols' opponents, and took forty years to break. The double fortress of Xiangyang on the Han river held out from 1268 to 1273 and fell only to counterweight trebuchets built by engineers brought from Persia. Hangzhou, the largest city in the world, surrendered in 1276; the last Song loyalists were destroyed at the naval battle of Yamen in 1279, where an official is said to have jumped into the sea carrying the child emperor.

steps.name: The invasions of Japan
steps.page: Kublai sent two seaborne invasions against Japan, in 1274 and in 1281. The second was much the larger; the sources describe some 4,000 ships and 140,000 men, in two fleets from Korea and southern China. Both were held on the beaches of Kyushu by the defenders and then wrecked by typhoons, which Japanese tradition named *kamikaze*, divine winds. Campaigns against Vietnam, Champa and Java also failed.

steps.name: Four khanates
steps.page: Kublai died in 1294 as emperor of China and nominal Great Khan of an empire that no longer acknowledged him. The Golden Horde, the Chagatai khanate and the Ilkhanate were by then independent states, at war with one another as often as with anybody else, and each was being absorbed by the culture it governed: the Ilkhans and the Horde became Muslim, the Yuan Chinese. The unified empire had lasted a little under ninety years.

name: Genghis Khan proclaimed
summary: Temüjin was proclaimed supreme ruler of the Mongol confederacy at an assembly (kurultai) and took the title Genghis Khan.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). In 1206 an assembly of the tribes of the eastern steppe, held on the Onon river, acclaimed [Temüjin](item:temujin-genghis-khan) as their ruler and gave him the title Genghis Khan. It was the formal act that turned twenty years of steppe warfare into a single state, and it is the point from which the Mongol conquests are dated.

Temüjin had spent those years destroying, absorbing or outmanoeuvring the confederations around him, among them the Merkit, Tatar, Kereit and Naiman, often against former sworn brothers and patrons. The assembly, a *kurultai*, was the traditional way a steppe leader was recognised, and the title he took is usually read as universal or oceanic ruler.

He then broke the defeated tribes up and redistributed their men into units of ten, hundred, thousand and ten thousand under officers he appointed himself, which cut the old tribal loyalties out of the army. He formed a personal guard from the sons of his commanders, adopted the Uyghur script for writing Mongol, set up a relay post system across the steppe, and issued a body of rulings, the *yassa*, that bound his own family as well as everyone else.

Within three years the new state was at war with the Western Xia; within five, with the Jin empire of northern China.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan).

name: Magna Carta
summary: English barons forced King John to accept written limits on royal power at Runnymede.
body:
On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede on the Thames, King John of England accepted a charter of liberties put to him by rebel barons. Magna Carta, the Great Charter, bound a king to written rules. The claim implicit in it, that a ruler is under the law rather than above it, has been quoted ever since.

Most of its sixty-three clauses were the immediate grievances of the men who wrote it: what the crown could take from an heir, how widows and wards were to be treated, the extent of the royal forests, the seizure of goods and horses without payment, the removal of foreign mercenaries. The general clauses came near the end, and two of them lasted. One forbade the imprisonment or dispossession of a free man except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land; the other promised that justice would not be sold, delayed or denied to anyone.

It failed at once. John had the charter annulled by Pope Innocent III within ten weeks and civil war followed. What saved it was John's death in 1216: his young son's regents reissued the charter to gather support, and it was reissued repeatedly through the century until it entered English statute law in 1297.

Seventeenth-century lawyers, Edward Coke above all, used it against the Stuart kings as though it had always been a general guarantee of liberty. Through them it reached the American colonies, and its language is visible in the [United States constitution](event:us-constitution) and its Bill of Rights. Four copies of the 1215 charter survive.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Carta).

name: Order of Preachers founded
summary: Dominic founded an order of friars to preach against heresy; it became a major intellectual force in the medieval Church.
body:
The Order of Preachers, commonly called the Dominicans, was confirmed by Pope Honorius III in 1216. Dominic de Guzmán, a Castilian canon, had founded it at Toulouse to preach against the Cathar heresy in southern France, and it became the leading teaching order of the medieval church.

Dominic held that the Cathars were being answered badly. Church delegations arrived with retinues, horses and property to argue against preachers who owned nothing, and lost the argument on sight. He proposed men who would live by begging as the Cathar *perfecti* did, and who would be trained in theology well enough to win the debate: friars rather than monks, living in towns, moving between them, and studying rather than farming.

The order grew quickly and attached itself to the new [universities](event:university-bologna). Albertus Magnus and his pupil Thomas Aquinas were Dominicans, and much of [scholasticism](event:scholasticism) was written by them; so, later and very differently, were Meister Eckhart and, in the sixteenth century, Bartolomé de las Casas, who argued against the enslavement of the peoples of the Americas.

The same competence made them the church's investigators. Dominicans staffed much of the medieval Inquisition and later the Spanish and Roman ones, and the order acquired a reputation it has never entirely lost, along with a Latin pun on its name, *Domini canes*, the hounds of the Lord.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Order).

name: Mali Empire
summary: A West African kingdom that controlled the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt, and made Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning.
body:
Mali was a West African empire that grew out of the Mandé chiefdoms of the upper Niger in the thirteenth century and dominated the western Sudan for about two hundred years. It controlled the southern end of the trans-Saharan routes, and the gold that moved along them made its rulers the wealthiest in the region. Its scholars and its gold together made Timbuktu famous in the Islamic world and, eventually, in Europe.

Its founder, Sundiata Keita, is known chiefly through an epic recited by griots and written down much later; the documentary record is thin and rests largely on the Arabic writers al-Umari and Ibn Battuta, who visited in 1352. Sundiata is said to have defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina about 1235 and to have bound the Mandé clans under a charter of rules.

The empire's wealth came from control rather than production. The gold was mined at Bambuk and Bure by peoples outside Mali's rule, and Mali taxed it as it passed north, exchanging it for Saharan salt, cloth, horses, copper and books. Its rulers were Muslim while most of their subjects were not, and the [pilgrimage of Mansa Musa](event:mansa-musa) in 1324 made both the wealth and the religion visible as far away as Cairo.

Mali lost its northern provinces to Tuareg raiding and to the rise of [Songhai](event:songhai-empire) in the fifteenth century, and had shrunk to a small kingdom on the upper Niger by 1600.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali_Empire).

name: Sukhothai Kingdom
summary: A Thai kingdom on the upper Chao Phraya produced a distinctive Buddhist art style and the earliest known writing in Thai script.
body:
Sukhothai was a Thai kingdom on the upper Chao Phraya plain, conventionally dated from 1238, when Si Inthrathit is said to have thrown off Khmer overlordship, until its absorption by Ayutthaya in 1438. Thai tradition treats it as the first Thai state, and its art and its script as the classical forms of both.

It emerged as the Khmer empire's grip on the region loosened and Tai-speaking peoples settled the river valleys. Its best-known ruler, Ram Khamhaeng, reigned from about 1279 to 1298 and extended its influence far down the peninsula and into what is now Laos, mostly as tribute rather than direct rule. He opened relations with Yuan China, from which Sukhothai's celadon potters are said to have learned their craft.

The stone stele attributed to him, dated 1292 and found in 1833, describes a kingdom of free trade, accessible justice and a king who could be petitioned by ringing a bell at his gate; it is also the oldest known document in Thai script. Its authenticity has been disputed since the 1980s, and while most scholars accept it, the argument has not closed.

Theravada Buddhism was established in this period from Sri Lankan monks, Sukhothai's walking Buddha figures, elongated, smooth and shown mid-stride, are treated as the classical form of Thai sculpture. Ayutthaya reduced the kingdom to a tributary in 1349 and annexed it outright in 1438.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhothai_Kingdom).

name: Mongol sack of Baghdad
summary: Hulagu's army destroyed the Abbasid capital, killed the caliph and ended the [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age) in Iraq.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). In February 1258 a Mongol army under Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, took Baghdad after a siege of about two weeks, killed the last Abbasid caliph and destroyed much of the city. It ended a caliphate that had held nominal authority over the Sunni world for five centuries, and it is the conventional close of the [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age).

Hulagu had been sent west with a large army and explicit instructions to reduce the states of the region. He destroyed the Nizari Ismaili strongholds in the Alborz mountains in 1256, then demanded submission from the caliph al-Musta'sim, who refused and had no army capable of backing the refusal. Mongol engineers breached the eastern wall; the caliph surrendered on 10 February and was executed a few days later, by tradition rolled in a carpet and trampled so that no royal blood would touch the ground.

The number killed is given by the sources as anything from tens of thousands to eight hundred thousand; the low end is the credible one, and the city was still substantial afterwards. The lasting damage was to the libraries, the canals and the irrigation works of lower Iraq, and Baghdad was never again the capital of anything larger than a province.

The Abbasid line was continued as a figurehead in Cairo under the Mamluks, who stopped the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut two years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(1258)).

layers.label: Hulagu came west, destroying the Nizari strongholds in the Alborz in 1256

name: Yuan dynasty founded
summary: Kublai Khan completed the conquest of Song China and ruled it as a Chinese emperor from Dadu, modern Beijing.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271, took the last Song capital in 1276 and completed the conquest of southern China in 1279. For the first time the whole of China was ruled by a foreign dynasty, and for the first time in three centuries it was ruled as one state.

Kublai governed as a Chinese emperor rather than as a steppe khan. He built a new capital at Dadu, modern Beijing, on a Chinese plan, took a dynastic name from the *Book of Changes*, adopted the Song bureaucracy and its tax registers, and extended the Grand Canal so that the rice of the south could feed the north. His claim to be Great Khan of the whole Mongol empire was not accepted by the western khanates, which by then were separate states in all but name.

Mongol rule was also a system of ranks. The population was sorted into four classes, with Mongols at the top and the former subjects of the Song at the bottom; senior office went to Mongols and to Central Asian and Persian administrators rather than to Chinese scholars, and the examinations were suspended for decades. Foreign merchants, envoys and missionaries were welcome, which is the China [Marco Polo](event:marco-polo) described.

Inflation of the paper currency, factional killing at court, catastrophic flooding of the Yellow River and the [Black Death](event:black-death) broke the dynasty within a century. Rebel armies took Dadu in 1368 and founded the [Ming](event:ming-dynasty).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty).

name: Travels of Marco Polo
summary: A Venetian merchant's account of twenty years in Asia became medieval Europe's main window on China.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant who left for Asia with his father and uncle in 1271, spent some seventeen years in the lands of Kublai Khan, and returned in 1295. The account he afterwards dictated was medieval Europe's fullest description of China, and remained so for two hundred years.

His father and uncle had already made one journey east and were going back with letters from the pope; Marco, about seventeen when they set out, went with them. They travelled by way of Acre, Persia and the Pamirs, and reached Kublai's court around 1275. Polo says he was employed as an envoy and administrator, which would have taken him through much of the empire; the Chinese records do not mention him, and a minority of scholars doubt he went as far as he claimed. The family came home by sea from southern China, escorting a Mongol bride to Persia.

The book was written down in 1298 by Rustichello of Pisa, a writer of romances, while the two were prisoners of Genoa after a naval defeat. It describes the size and order of Chinese cities, paper money, coal burnt as fuel, the postal relay system and the wealth of the court, and reports at second hand on Japan, India, Africa and the spice islands. Contemporaries called it *Il Milione* and largely disbelieved it. It was copied and read widely nonetheless, was used by European mapmakers for two centuries, and [Columbus](event:columbus) owned a copy annotated in his own hand.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Polo).

name: Fall of Acre
summary: Acre, the last crusader stronghold on the Levantine mainland, fell to the Mamluks.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). Acre, the capital and chief port of what remained of the kingdom of Jerusalem, fell to the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil on 18 May 1291 after a siege of six weeks. Its loss ended the Latin presence on the Levantine mainland, just under two centuries after the [First Crusade](event:first-crusade) took Jerusalem.

The crusader states had survived their reduction to a coastal strip largely because their neighbours were divided. That ended with the Mamluk sultans of Egypt, who had stopped the Mongols in 1260 and then took the Latin castles and towns one at a time: Caesarea and Arsuf in 1265, Antioch in 1268, Krak des Chevaliers in 1271, Tripoli in 1289. The truce that still covered Acre was broken when newly arrived crusaders from Italy killed Muslim merchants in the city.

The garrison, made up of the military orders, the Italian communes, a small royal force and volunteers, held the double walls against mining and bombardment until 18 May, when the Accursed Tower was carried. Part of the population got away by sea; most did not. The Templar compound on the shore held out for several days more and then collapsed, killing defenders and attackers together.

Khalil had the surviving fortified ports dismantled so that no fleet could use them again. Cyprus took in the refugees and the orders. Crusades continued to be preached for centuries, but no Latin state was ever re-established in Syria or Palestine.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Acre_(1291)).

name: Majapahit Empire
summary: A Javanese kingdom founded in 1293 became the dominant maritime power of the archipelago, claiming tribute from Sumatra to New Guinea.
body:
Majapahit was a Javanese kingdom founded in 1293 that became the dominant maritime power of the Indonesian archipelago during the fourteenth century. Its capital stood inland in east Java, near modern Trowulan, and its wealth came from rice and from control of the trade in spices, cloth and porcelain moving through the Java Sea.

It was founded out of a Mongol invasion. Kublai Khan sent a fleet to punish the Javanese king Kertanegara, who had mutilated his envoy; by the time it arrived Kertanegara was dead, and his son-in-law Raden Wijaya used the Mongols against his rival and then turned on them, driving them out and taking the throne in 1293.

Its height came under Hayam Wuruk, who reigned from 1350 to 1389, and his chief minister Gajah Mada, who served from 1334 to 1364 and swore an oath, the *Palapa*, not to taste spices until the archipelago was united. The court poem *Nagarakretagama* of 1365 lists ninety-eight tributaries from Sumatra to New Guinea. Historians treat that as a claim rather than a description: direct rule probably reached little beyond east Java and Bali, and the rest was tribute, a trade monopoly, or nothing at all.

Its religion was a Javanese fusion of Shaivism and Buddhism, and its literature and law shaped Java long afterwards. Civil war after 1404 weakened it, the Muslim ports of the north coast grew independent, and the sultanate of Demak ended it in 1527. Twentieth-century Indonesian nationalists took it as the precedent for a single archipelagic state.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majapahit).

name: Ottoman Empire
summary: From a frontier principality in Anatolia the Ottomans built an empire across the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa that lasted six centuries.
body:
The Ottoman Empire began as one of the small Turkish frontier principalities in north-western Anatolia, conventionally dated from Osman I in 1299, and grew into a state that ruled the Balkans, Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt, Mesopotamia and North Africa for six centuries. It ended in 1922, when the sultanate was abolished after defeat in [the First World War](event:ww1).

Its early advantage was position: on the Byzantine frontier, able to draw fighting men from across Anatolia, and across the straits into Europe from the 1350s. The Ottomans took Adrianople in 1361 and had reduced Byzantium to its capital and a few outposts long before Mehmed II [took Constantinople](event:fall-constantinople) in 1453 and made it his own capital. Under Selim I the empire absorbed the Mamluk sultanate in 1516–17, taking Syria, Egypt and the guardianship of Mecca and Medina; under Suleiman, who ruled from 1520 to 1566, it took Hungary, besieged Vienna and dominated the eastern Mediterranean.

It was governed by an apparatus with no European parallel: a standing infantry corps, the janissaries, and much of the senior administration recruited as boys from Christian villages in the Balkans and converted; a codified sultanic law running alongside religious law; and an arrangement that left the Orthodox, Armenian and Jewish communities to run their own religious and civil affairs under their own leaders. Its cities took in the Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492.

Its decline was slow and is often dated too early, but from 1699 the empire lost territory in almost every war it fought. The nineteenth century brought Greek, Serbian and Balkan independence, Russian pressure, heavy foreign debt, and a programme of reform, the Tanzimat, that reorganised the army, the law and the schools without arresting the losses. Defeat in 1918 left Anatolia occupied; the resistance that followed produced the Turkish republic in 1923, and the borders that Britain and France drew across the Arab provinces are much of the modern map of the Middle East.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire).

name: Little Ice Age
summary: A few tenths of a degree of cooling in the northern hemisphere brought advancing glaciers, frozen rivers and repeated harvest failures.
body:
The Little Ice Age was a period of cooler climate in the northern hemisphere, conventionally placed between about 1300 and 1850, though the dates are disputed and some scholars prefer a shorter span beginning in the sixteenth century. It was not an ice age. Northern hemisphere temperatures were less than 1 °C below late-twentieth-century levels, and the cooling was uneven in both time and place.

Several causes have been proposed and none alone accounts for it: a cluster of large sulphur-rich volcanic eruptions from 1257 onward; repeated periods of low solar activity, among them the Spörer minimum of about 1400–1550 and the Maunder minimum of 1645–1715; changes in ocean circulation; and the regrowth of forest on farmland emptied by the [Black Death](event:black-death) and by [the epidemics that followed contact with the Americas](event:americas-epidemics).

Its effects are best recorded in Europe. Alpine glaciers advanced far enough to destroy farms and villages in the seventeenth century; sea ice closed Icelandic harbours; the Thames froze hard enough to carry frost fairs between 1608 and 1814; and cold wet summers produced famines, among them the Great Famine of 1315–17 and the French and Scandinavian famines of the 1690s, which killed roughly a tenth of the population of several countries. The Norse settlements in Greenland were abandoned, the last surviving document from them dating to 1412.

Whether it was global is disputed. The IPCC concluded that the cold periods recorded in different regions were not synchronous, and the term is now generally used of the northern hemisphere rather than of the planet.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Ice_Age).

name: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: The ruler of Mali crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage with so much gold that he depressed its price in Cairo for years.
body:
Mansa Musa, ruler of the [Mali empire](event:mali-empire), crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324. He travelled with an enormous retinue and with so much gold, which he gave away and spent freely in Cairo, that Arabic writers report the price of gold there was depressed for years afterwards. The journey put Mali into the historical record of the Islamic world and, in time, of Europe.

Mali's wealth came from taxing the gold that moved north across the desert from the Bambuk and Bure fields. The pilgrimage was a religious obligation and a piece of statecraft at once: it announced a Muslim king of a large and rich country to the scholars and rulers of Cairo, Mecca and Medina, and Musa came home with jurists, books and architects. The Andalusian Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, who returned with him, is associated with building work at Timbuktu and Gao.

Timbuktu grew over the following centuries into a centre of Islamic scholarship, with the Sankoré mosque at its heart and a copying trade that supplied the whole Sahel. Tens of thousands of its manuscripts survive.

The account of the journey travelled too. It reached the chroniclers of Cairo and through them the mapmakers of Europe: the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows a crowned king seated in the western Sudan holding out a gold nugget, named as the lord of the mines of Guinea. It is the image by which Mali entered European geography.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa).

name: Tenochtitlan founded
summary: The Mexica built their capital on an island in Lake Texcoco; it became one of the largest cities in the world.
body:
Tenochtitlan was founded on an island in Lake Texcoco, in the valley of Mexico, by the Mexica in 1325. Within two centuries it was the capital of the [Aztec empire](event:aztec-empire) and one of the largest cities in the world, with a population usually estimated between 150,000 and 200,000.

The Mexica were latecomers to the valley, remembered in their own histories as a poor migrant people who had served other city-states as mercenaries and were pushed onto the marshy islands nobody else wanted. Their founding story tells of a sign promised by their god Huitzilopochtli, an eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus, seen at the place where they were to settle. The eagle and the cactus are on the flag of Mexico.

Causeways with removable bridges joined the island to the shore and made the city defensible; an aqueduct from Chapultepec brought drinking water; a dyke ten kilometres long kept the brackish eastern water off the fresher western side; and *chinampas*, rectangular plots built up from lake mud between stakes, produced several crops a year. Canoes carried everything, there being no draught animals.

At the centre stood a walled precinct holding the twin-shrined Templo Mayor. The Spanish soldiers who saw the city in 1519 compared it to Venice and to the enchanted cities in their romances. They [destroyed it](event:spanish-conquest) in 1521, and Mexico City was built on the rubble.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenochtitlan).

name: Hundred Years' War
summary: England and France fought intermittently for 116 years over the French crown.
body:
The Hundred Years' War was a series of conflicts between England and France, fought between 1337 and 1453 over the English kings' lands in France and their claim to the French throne. It was not continuous: long truces separated the campaigns, and the fighting came in bursts of a few years at a time. France won, and England was left with nothing on the continent except Calais.

The quarrel had two roots. English kings had held territory in France since 1066 and held it as vassals of the French crown, an arrangement neither side found tolerable; and when the direct Capetian line failed in 1328, Edward III of England had a claim through his mother that the French rejected. Philip VI confiscated Aquitaine on 24 May 1337, and Edward answered by claiming the crown itself.

The English won the famous battles and could not hold the country. Dismounted men-at-arms and massed longbowmen destroyed larger French armies at [Crécy](event:crecy), Poitiers and [Agincourt](event:agincourt), and the *chevauchée*, a fast destructive ride through the countryside, was used to ruin the enemy's tax base rather than to take ground. But garrisoning what had been ridden through was expensive, and the French learned to refuse battle, to besiege methodically, and at last to shoot back: Castillon in 1453 was decided by French field artillery.

The war changed both kingdoms. France came out of it centralised, taxed by a permanent levy and defended by the first standing army in western Europe. England came out of it in debt and in the factional conflict that ran on into the Wars of the Roses. In both, a war begun by kings over an inheritance was paid for by grants from parliaments and estates.

The phases are listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War).

steps.name: Aquitaine confiscated
steps.page: On 24 May 1337 Philip VI declared the duchy of Aquitaine forfeit, on the ground that Edward III had sheltered his enemy Robert of Artois. Edward, who held Aquitaine as a vassal of the French crown and had a claim to that crown through his mother Isabella, answered by assuming the title of king of France in 1340. The dispute was old; the confiscation is the act from which the war is dated.

steps.name: Battle of Sluys
steps.page: On 24 June 1340 the English fleet destroyed a French one crowded into the harbour of Sluys, on the Flemish coast. The French ships were chained together and fought as a platform for archers and men-at-arms; the English took almost all of them. The victory gave England command of the Channel for a generation, which meant the war would be fought in France.

steps.name: The siege of Calais
steps.page: Edward marched from Crécy to Calais and settled down to starve it out, building a town of huts around the walls and blockading the harbour. It held for eleven months and surrendered on 3 August 1347; the story of the six burghers who came out with ropes around their necks and were spared at the queen's request comes from Froissart. Edward expelled most of the population and settled English there. Calais remained English until 1558, and was the bridgehead for every later campaign.

steps.name: Battle of Poitiers
steps.page: On 19 September 1356 Edward's son, the Black Prince, was caught returning from a *chevauchée* through central France and fought on ground of his own choosing near Poitiers. The result was Crécy repeated, with one addition: King John II of France was captured. His ransom was set at three million gold crowns, and France, leaderless and taxed for it, fell into peasant revolt and factional government.

steps.name: Treaty of Brétigny
steps.page: Agreed on 8 May 1360 and ratified at Calais in October, the treaty gave Edward an enlarged Aquitaine in full sovereignty, together with Calais and Ponthieu, in return for renouncing his claim to the French crown and to Normandy, Anjou, Touraine and Maine. The renunciations were left to be exchanged later and never were, which allowed both sides to reopen the war when it suited them.

steps.name: The French recovery
steps.page: Charles V reopened the war in 1369 and won it back without fighting a general engagement. His constable, Bertrand du Guesclin, took castles and towns one at a time and refused battle; Castilian galleys raided the English coast; the English *chevauchées* rode through France and achieved nothing. By 1380 the English held only Calais, Bordeaux, Bayonne and a few ports. The truce of Leulinghem in June 1389 closed the phase with both kingdoms exhausted and both about to fall into internal crisis.

steps.name: Treaty of Troyes
steps.page: Henry V's victory and the murder of John the Fearless brought Burgundy into the English camp and left the French court, under an intermittently insane king, unable to resist. By the treaty of 21 May 1420 Henry married Charles VI's daughter Catherine and was recognised as heir to the French throne, disinheriting the dauphin. Both kings died in 1422, leaving the infant Henry VI as claimant to both kingdoms, and a rival French court south of the Loire.

steps.name: Formigny, Castillon and the end
steps.page: Burgundy left the English alliance at Arras in 1435, and Charles VII rebuilt his army around paid companies and a corps of gunners under the Bureau brothers. Normandy was retaken in a fourteen-month campaign that ended at Formigny in April 1450, where French cannon broke the English line. Guyenne followed: at Castillon, on 17 July 1453, an English army attacked an entrenched artillery park and was destroyed, and the English commander John Talbot was killed. Bordeaux surrendered on 19 October. No treaty was signed; the fighting simply stopped.

name: Alhambra Palace
summary: The Nasrid emirs of Granada built a palace complex that combined Islamic architecture with local Iberian craft traditions.
body:
Part of [The Reconquista](event:reconquista). The Alhambra is a palace and fortress complex on a ridge above Granada, built mainly in the fourteenth century by the Nasrid emirs of the last Muslim state in Iberia. Its carved stucco, tile mosaic, worked wood and courtyards built around water are generally taken as the high point of Islamic art in western Europe.

The site had been fortified since the ninth century. The Nasrids, who ruled Granada from 1238 as tributaries of Castile, turned it into a royal city with its own mosque, baths, workshops, water supply and garrison. The palaces that survive were built under Yusuf I and Muhammad V between about 1333 and 1391: the Court of the Myrtles around a still reflecting pool, the Court of the Lions with its arcade of slender columns and a fountain carried on twelve stone lions, and the Hall of the Two Sisters beneath a vault of some five thousand *muqarnas* cells.

Its walls are covered in writing. Quranic verses, dynastic mottoes and Arabic poems composed for particular rooms are worked into the plaster, among them the Nasrid motto repeated everywhere: there is no victor but God.

The complex passed to the Castilian crown when [Granada surrendered](event:granada) in 1492. Charles V demolished part of it for a Renaissance palace that was never roofed; the rest was neglected, occupied by squatters and damaged by Napoleon's troops, before nineteenth-century travellers, Washington Irving among them, made its restoration a cause.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra).

name: Black Death
summary: The deadliest pandemic in recorded history killed between a third and a half of the population of Europe between 1346 and 1353.
body:
The Black Death was a pandemic of plague that killed a large part of the population of Europe, western Asia and North Africa between 1346 and 1353. Estimates of the European death toll range from a quarter to two thirds of the population; a third to a half is the usual figure, and Europe did not return to its earlier numbers for about two hundred years. It is the deadliest pandemic in recorded history.

The disease was caused by the bacterium *Yersinia pestis*, which was not identified until Alexandre Yersin isolated it during an outbreak in Hong Kong in 1894. Genetic work on medieval burials has since confirmed it in the fourteenth-century dead and traced the strain's ancestor to Central Asia, where tombstones in the Chu valley of present-day Kyrgyzstan record a spike in deaths from "pestilence" in 1338 and 1339. How it then spread is still argued about: the classic account has it carried by rat fleas, while more recent work holds that the speed of the medieval spread fits human fleas, body lice and person-to-person pneumonic transmission better.

It reached Europe along the trade routes. Plague was in the Golden Horde army besieging the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea in 1346, and Genoese ships carried it to Constantinople in the summer of 1347 and to Sicily that October. From the Italian ports it took about three years to cross the continent, moving faster along coasts and rivers than overland.

Nobody knew what it was. Explanations ran from a conjunction of the planets to corrupted air to divine punishment, and the responses from quarantine (Ragusa's thirty-day isolation of arriving ships in 1377 gave the word its name) to flagellant processions and to the massacre of Jewish communities accused of poisoning wells.

The demographic shock rearranged the economy. Land was suddenly plentiful and labour scarce; wages rose, rents fell, and attempts to legislate wages back down met resistance, of which the English rising of 1381 was one instance. Serfdom weakened across much of western Europe, and plague itself did not go away: it returned in waves every decade or two for three hundred years.

Its course across Europe is traced in the steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death).

steps.name: The siege of Caffa
steps.page: Plague was already moving west along the caravan routes from Central Asia when it reached the army of Jani Beg, khan of the Golden Horde, besieging the Genoese trading colony of Caffa in the Crimea. The chronicler Gabriele de' Mussi, writing at second hand, says the besiegers catapulted their own dead over the walls; historians treat the detail with caution but not the outbreak. Genoese ships left the port for home.

steps.name: Constantinople and the Black Sea
steps.page: The disease arrived in Constantinople in the summer of 1347, the first place in Europe it is recorded. The emperor John VI Kantakouzenos, whose own son died of it, wrote a description of the symptoms modelled on Thucydides. From the Bosphorus it went with shipping in every direction at once: to the Aegean, to Alexandria, and westward along the Mediterranean sea lanes.

steps.name: Twelve galleys at Messina
steps.page: In October 1347 twelve Genoese galleys put in at Messina in Sicily with dying crews. The town expelled them, which spread the infection along the coast rather than containing it, and the whole island was affected within months. Sicily is the entry point from which the pandemic's course through western Europe is usually traced.

steps.name: Alexandria, Cairo and the Levant
steps.page: Ships out of the Black Sea carried plague to Alexandria in the autumn of 1347, and from there it went up the Nile and across the Levant. Cairo, then one of the largest cities in the world, is reported to have lost between a third and two fifths of its people within eight months. Mortality across the Middle East is generally put at about a third, comparable to the European figure.

steps.name: Genoa, Venice, Pisa and Marseille
steps.page: Galleys from Caffa reached Genoa and Venice in January 1348. The outbreak that followed a few weeks later at Pisa was the entry into northern Italy, and one of the ships driven out of an Italian harbour carried the plague to Marseille at the end of the same month. Florence, whose losses Boccaccio described in the introduction to the *Decameron*, fell from something over 110,000 people to about 50,000 by 1351.

steps.name: France, Iberia and England
steps.page: From Marseille the plague went up the Rhône to Avignon, where the pope's physician Guy de Chauliac stayed and wrote about it, and across Languedoc into Spain. It reached the south coast of England in the summer of 1348 and London by the autumn. Paris is estimated to have lost half of its hundred thousand people. Governments responded chiefly by trying to hold wages and prices where they had been.

steps.name: Attacks on Jewish communities
steps.page: From late 1348 a rumour that Jews had poisoned the wells spread through the Rhineland, Alsace, Switzerland and the Empire, in several places arriving before the plague itself did. Whole communities were burnt or expelled; about two thousand people were killed at Strasbourg in February 1349, before the plague had reached the town at all. Pope Clement VI issued two bulls against the accusation and could not stop it. Many survivors migrated east into Poland and Lithuania.

steps.name: Germany, Scotland and Scandinavia
steps.page: Through 1349 and 1350 the plague worked north and east through the German lands, into Scotland, and by sea to Scandinavia: a ship put in at Askøy in 1349 and the outbreak spread from Bjørgvin, modern Bergen, over the whole of Norway. Hamburg and Bremen are each thought to have lost at least three fifths of their inhabitants. Iceland and Greenland were reached later or, in Greenland's case, perhaps not at all.

steps.name: Northern Russia and Moscow
steps.page: The pandemic completed a circuit. Having entered Europe from the Black Sea, it arrived in northern Russia only in 1352, reaching Novgorod and Pskov by way of the Baltic, and Moscow in 1353, where it killed the grand prince and his family. That is the conventional end of the first wave. Plague returned to Europe in 1361, in 1374, and every decade or two thereafter until the eighteenth century.

name: Battle of Crécy
summary: English longbowmen destroyed the French cavalry, an early sign that armoured knights were losing their dominance.
body:
Part of [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war). At Crécy in Picardy on 26 August 1346, an English army under Edward III destroyed a much larger French force under Philip VI. It was the first great English victory of the war, and the battle that made the reputation of the longbow.

Edward had landed in Normandy in July and ridden across northern France burning as he went, a *chevauchée* meant to ruin the French king's revenues and force him to give battle. Caught north of the Somme, Edward chose ground on a slope near Crécy-en-Ponthieu, dismounted his men-at-arms and put his archers on the flanks in front of them.

The French came up late in the day and attacked piecemeal. Their Genoese crossbowmen, without the pavises that should have covered them and shooting uphill into the sun, were shot down and then ridden through by their own cavalry, who charged repeatedly into arrow fire and into pits the English had dug. The dead included the blind king of Bohemia, who had had his horse tied to those of his companions so that he could take part, and a large part of the French nobility present.

The English then besieged Calais, which fell in 1347 and stayed English until 1558. Crécy is often described as the end of the dominance of the armoured knight. Historians more often read it as showing what a disciplined army of dismounted men-at-arms and archers, on ground of its own choosing, could do to one that attacked without order.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Crécy).

name: Duchy of Burgundy at its height
summary: A wealthy principality between France and the Holy Roman Empire, Burgundy became a centre of art, music and courtly culture.
body:
The Valois dukes of Burgundy ruled, between 1363 and 1477, an assemblage of territories running from the Swiss border to the North Sea. It was never a kingdom and never one country: the duchy of Burgundy was a French fief, the lands in the Low Countries were held of the Holy Roman Emperor, and the two halves did not touch. For a century it was nonetheless one of the richest and most admired courts in Europe.

It began in 1363, when John II of France granted the duchy to his youngest son, Philip the Bold. Philip's marriage to the heiress of Flanders brought in the cloth towns of the north, and his successors John the Fearless, Philip the Good and Charles the Bold added Brabant, Holland, Hainaut, Luxembourg and more by inheritance, purchase and war. Burgundy's alliance with England during the [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war), and its change of sides at Arras in 1435, decided much of that conflict.

The court's wealth went into display and patronage: the Order of the Golden Fleece, founded in 1430; the composers Dufay and Binchois; and the painters of the southern Netherlands, among them Jan van Eyck, who was Philip the Good's *valet de chambre*, and Rogier van der Weyden.

Charles the Bold spent his reign trying to weld the two halves into a kingdom and was killed besieging Nancy in 1477. France seized the duchy itself; his daughter Mary's marriage to Maximilian of Habsburg carried the Low Countries into the Habsburg inheritance, and with them the wars of the following century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Burgundy).

name: Ming dynasty
summary: Han Chinese rule was restored after the Mongols; the Forbidden City was built, treasure fleets sailed, and the Great Wall took the form seen today.
body:
The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, after Chinese rebels drove out the Mongol [Yuan](event:yuan-dynasty). It was the last dynasty ruled by a Han Chinese house, and one of the most stable: a period of population growth, commercial expansion, and a state that reached further into ordinary life than any before it.

Its founder, the Hongwu emperor, had been an orphaned peasant and a novice monk before he was a rebel general, and he governed with a suspicion of officials that never left him. He abolished the office of chancellor and took the administration into his own hands, purged tens of thousands in a series of treason cases, registered the whole population by household and occupation, and tried to build a self-sufficient agrarian order of villages and hereditary military colonies.

His son the Yongle emperor reversed much of the caution. He moved the capital north to Beijing and built the [Forbidden City](event:forbidden-city) there, repaired the Grand Canal, commissioned an encyclopedia of some 11,000 volumes, and sent [Zheng He's fleets](event:zheng-he) across the Indian Ocean. The voyages were stopped after 1433 and never resumed.

The later Ming turned defensive. The [Great Wall](event:great-wall) was rebuilt in brick and stone, in the form visitors see today, against Mongol raiding that reached the walls of Beijing in 1550. At the same time the economy became thoroughly commercial and was increasingly monetised in silver, much of it American and arriving by way of Manila, which tied Chinese prices to distant mines. Porcelain, printed books, drama and the novel all reached a wider public than ever before.

A run of famines, a collapse in silver imports, peasant rebellion and Manchu pressure on the northern frontier ended it. Rebels took Beijing in 1644 and the last Ming emperor hanged himself; the Manchus entered the city the same year and founded the Qing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty).

name: Zheng He
summary: Ming admiral who commanded seven state expeditions across the Indian Ocean, reaching Arabia and the East African coast.
body:
Born Ma He into a Muslim family in Yunnan, he was captured as a boy during the Ming conquest of the province, castrated, and placed in the household of the prince who became the Yongle Emperor. He rose to command the imperial fleet and was given the name Zheng He.

Between 1405 and 1433 he led [seven voyages](item:zheng-he) with fleets of up to 300 vessels and 27,000 men. The purpose was diplomatic rather than territorial: to enrol distant rulers in the tribute system, to carry envoys, and to display the reach of the [Ming](item:ming-dynasty). The fleets touched Java, Sri Lanka, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden and Malindi, and returned with ambassadors, spices and a giraffe.

He died on the last voyage and was buried at sea. The court, facing costs and a renewed Mongol threat on the northern frontier, abandoned the expeditions and let the records lapse. The Portuguese entered the same [maritime routes](item:silk-roads) some seventy years afterwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zheng_He).

name: Metal movable type in Korea
summary: Korean foundries cast movable metal type; the *Jikji* of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed with it, decades before Gutenberg.
body:
The *Jikji*, printed at the Heungdeok temple near Cheongju in 1377, is the oldest surviving book known to have been printed with movable metal type. It is a Korean Buddhist anthology of the teachings of the Zen patriarchs, compiled by the monk Baegun, and it precedes the [Gutenberg Bible](event:gutenberg-42-line) by about seventy-eight years.

Korea inherited [woodblock printing](event:woodblock-printing) from China and used it on a very large scale: the Tripitaka Koreana, over 80,000 blocks cut in the thirteenth century, still survives. Movable type was a Chinese invention too, made in ceramic under the Song, but it was in Goryeo Korea that it was cast in bronze. Korean records describe metal-type printing of a ritual text in the 1230s, before the *Jikji*, although no copy of that book survives.

The technique was a state one. The Joseon dynasty founded a government type foundry in 1403, and King Sejong's reign produced both a series of improved fonts and, in 1443, the hangul alphabet, which suits movable type far better than Chinese characters do. Even so, printing in Korea stayed small in scale: it served the court, the bureaucracy and the monasteries rather than a book market, which is much of why it did not have the effects [printing in Europe](event:printing-press) had.

Only the second volume of the *Jikji* survives. A French diplomat bought it in Korea in the 1880s, and it is now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, where its ownership is disputed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jikji).

name: Medici banking and political power
summary: The Medici family turned banking wealth into political control of Florence and into patronage of Florentine artists and architects.
body:
The Medici bank, founded at Florence by Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici in 1397, was the largest and most respected financial institution in fifteenth-century Europe. The family turned the money it made into control of the Florentine republic, which they governed without holding office, and into patronage that paid for a great deal of what is now called the [Renaissance](event:renaissance).

The bank was organised as a set of partnerships at Rome, Venice, Naples, Milan and Geneva, and later Lyon, Bruges and London, each with its own capital and its own manager, which limited the damage any one branch could do to the rest. Its most profitable business was not lending at interest, which canon law forbade, but the bill of exchange, in which a loan was concealed inside a currency transaction, and the handling of the papal revenues of the whole of Latin Christendom.

Cosimo de' Medici, who took over in 1429, made himself the effective ruler of Florence through clients, marriages and control of who could stand for office. He commissioned Brunelleschi, Donatello and Fra Angelico, and paid for the library of San Marco. His grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent kept the political system and neglected the bank; Botticelli, Verrocchio and the young Michelangelo worked under his patronage.

The bank declined through poor branch managers, unrecoverable loans to princes, and Lorenzo's diversion of its funds to cover his own. It was close to collapse when Charles VIII of France invaded Italy in 1494; the Florentines expelled the family, which returned to the city later as dukes rather than as bankers.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Medici).

name: The Renaissance
summary: A revival of classical learning and a transformation of European art, architecture and thought, beginning in Florence.
body:
The Renaissance was a period of European cultural change, running roughly from the fourteenth century to the early seventeenth, in which the art, literature and learning of Greek and Roman antiquity were recovered, imitated and eventually surpassed. It began in the city-states of northern Italy, above all Florence, and spread across the continent. The name means rebirth and was applied to the period by nineteenth-century historians.

Its intellectual programme was humanism: the study of grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy from ancient sources read in the original, rather than through medieval commentary. Petrarch hunted lost manuscripts in monastic libraries; scholars learned Greek from Byzantine teachers and from refugees after [the fall of Constantinople](event:fall-constantinople) in 1453; Lorenzo Valla proved the Donation of Constantine a forgery by examining its Latin, which is textual criticism recognisably modern. Cheap books from [the printing press](event:printing-press) carried the results everywhere.

In art the change was technical as much as intellectual. Linear perspective was worked out by Brunelleschi and set down by Alberti; anatomy was studied by dissection; oil paint, developed in the Netherlands, allowed depth of colour and detail that tempera could not. The subjects remained largely religious, but the treatment was of individual human beings standing in a coherent space. [Leonardo](item:leonardo-da-vinci), Michelangelo, Raphael, Titian, Dürer and Bruegel all worked within a century of one another.

Florentine bankers, Venetian merchants, the dukes of Milan, Ferrara and Urbino, the kings of France and England, and the popes competed for artists as a form of politics. Julius II and Leo X between them commissioned the new St Peter's, the [Sistine ceiling](event:sistine-chapel) and Raphael's rooms.

The period was not a golden age for everybody in it: it contained plague, war, the sack of Rome in 1527, the witch trials, and the religious wars that followed the [Reformation](event:reformation). Historians have long questioned the sharp break the name implies, since the twelfth century had a recovery of ancient learning of its own.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance).

name: Johannes Gutenberg
summary: German goldsmith who assembled movable metal type, oil-based ink and the press into a system for printing books in quantity.
body:
Little is documented about Gutenberg beyond lawsuits. Born in Mainz to a patrician family, he worked as a goldsmith at Strasbourg, returned to Mainz, and borrowed heavily from Johann Fust to finance a secret enterprise.

No single component was new: [block printing](item:woodblock-printing) and [movable type in Korea](item:korea-movable-type) both came earlier. What he assembled was the combination of a hand mould that cast identical letters in a lead alloy at speed, an oil-based ink that would adhere to metal, and a screw press adapted from wine-making.

The [42-line Bible](item:gutenberg-42-line) of about 1455 proved it worked. Fust foreclosed the same year and took over the workshop, leaving Gutenberg with little; he died in Mainz with a small pension from the archbishop. Within fifty years [the press](item:printing-press) had spread across Europe and printed perhaps twenty million books.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Gutenberg).

name: Battle of Ankara
summary: Timur defeated and captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I near Ankara on 20 July 1402, breaking up the Ottoman state for a decade.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). Timur, ruler of an empire centred on Samarkand, invaded Anatolia in 1402 after a exchange of letters with the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I over refugee Turkmen princes and the borders of the two states.

The armies met on the Cubuk plain north east of Ankara on 20 July. Timur had reached the ground first and controlled the water. Anatolian contingents in the Ottoman army went over to their former princes during the battle. Bayezid was captured and died in captivity the following March.

Timur restored the Anatolian beyliks and withdrew. The Ottoman state broke into competing principalities under Bayezid's sons for eleven years, a period known as the Interregnum, until Mehmed I reunited it in 1413. The defeat postponed the Ottoman advance in Europe and gave Constantinople another fifty years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ankara).

name: Voyages of Zheng He
summary: Ming treasure fleets of hundreds of ships sailed to India, Arabia and East Africa decades before the Portuguese.
body:
Part of [Ming dynasty](event:ming-dynasty). Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court sent seven fleets into the Indian Ocean under the eunuch admiral [Zheng He](item:zheng-he-admiral). They were the largest naval expeditions the world had yet seen: Chinese sources describe over three hundred ships and some 27,000 men on the first voyage, at a time when a European expedition meant three or four vessels.

Their purpose was neither conquest nor trade in the European sense. The Yongle emperor, who had taken the throne in a civil war, wanted distant rulers enrolled in the tribute system and his own legitimacy displayed; the fleets carried envoys out and brought foreign ambassadors, exotic animals and formal submissions back. Where they fought, against a pirate fleet at Palembang and a usurper in Ceylon, it was to secure the route rather than to hold ground.

The voyages reached Champa, Java, Sumatra, Malacca, Ceylon, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden, Mogadishu and Malindi on the East African coast. A giraffe brought back from Africa was presented at court as a *qilin*, an auspicious beast. The sizes recorded for the largest treasure ships, over 120 metres, are doubted by naval historians, though the fleets were certainly very large.

After the Yongle emperor's death the court reconsidered the cost. The Mongol frontier needed money, officials had always resented the power of eunuchs, and the programme ended with the seventh voyage; Zheng He died on it or shortly after. Chinese merchants went on sailing, but the state withdrew from the sea some seventy years before the Portuguese arrived in it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_treasure_voyages).

name: Forbidden City built
summary: The Ming emperor built a palace complex at the heart of Beijing, its layout mirroring cosmic order and containing nearly 1,000 buildings.
body:
Part of [Ming dynasty](event:ming-dynasty). The Forbidden City is the palace complex at the centre of Beijing, built between 1406 and 1420 for the Yongle emperor when he moved the [Ming](event:ming-dynasty) capital north from Nanjing. It was the seat of the Chinese court for five centuries and twenty-four emperors of the Ming and Qing, and is the largest surviving group of wooden palace buildings in the world.

It covers 72 hectares inside a moat and a wall ten metres high, and holds around 980 buildings. Its plan is strictly symmetrical about a north–south axis, an outer court of three great ceremonial halls where the business of the state was done, an inner court of residences behind it, and yellow glazed roof tiles reserved to the emperor. The building is said to have used a million workers; timber was floated from the forests of the south-west, paving bricks were fired in Shandong, and the largest carved marble ramp was dragged from its quarry on roads of ice in winter.

"Forbidden" is literal. Entry without permission was a capital offence, and most of the population of Beijing lived their whole lives around a wall they never passed.

The last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in 1912 and was allowed to remain in the inner court until 1924. The complex opened as the Palace Museum in 1925. Much of the imperial art collection was evacuated during the war with Japan, and a large part of it is now in Taipei.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City).

name: Council of Constance
summary: The council held at Constance from 1414 to 1418 ended the Western Schism by deposing or accepting the resignation of three rival popes and electing Martin V. It also condemned Jan Hus, who was burned in 1415.
body:
The Council of Constance met from November 1414 to April 1418. It was called by the Pisan pope John XXIII under pressure from Sigismund, king of the Romans, to end the Western Schism, in which three men claimed the papacy at once.

The council deposed John XXIII and Benedict XIII, accepted the resignation of Gregory XII, and in November 1417 elected Martin V, who was accepted throughout Latin Christendom. In the decree Haec sancta it declared that a general council held its authority directly from Christ, a position later rejected by the papacy.

It also tried the Bohemian preacher [Jan Hus](event:jan-hus), who had come under a safe conduct from Sigismund. He was condemned and burned on 6 July 1415, and the remains of John Wycliffe were ordered exhumed and burned. The sentence on Hus was followed in Bohemia by the [Hussite Wars](event:hussite-wars).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Constance).

name: Battle of Agincourt
summary: Henry V's outnumbered and exhausted army routed the French in a muddy defile.
body:
Part of [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war). At Agincourt, in Artois, on 25 October 1415, the army of Henry V of England destroyed a much larger French force. It was the most one-sided of the English victories of the war, and it put Henry in a position to demand the French crown itself.

He had landed in Normandy in August and spent five weeks taking Harfleur, which cost him a third of his army to dysentery. He set out for Calais with the rest, perhaps six thousand men, most of them archers, and found the French, several times more numerous, across the road at Agincourt. Both sides stood facing each other for hours; Henry advanced first and provoked the attack.

The ground was decisive. A recently ploughed field, soaked by rain, lay between two woods, so the French had to come on over a narrowing front, in armour, through mud, into archery. The leading ranks were pushed forward by the press behind them until they could not use their weapons, and men who fell were trampled or smothered in the churned ground. French casualties, including much of the nobility of northern France, were very heavy. Henry ordered the killing of prisoners during the battle, believing a fresh attack was coming; his own heralds recorded the order without comment, and commentators have argued about it since.

The victory led to the conquest of Normandy and to the Treaty of Troyes in 1420, which made Henry heir to the French throne. He died two years later, aged thirty-five.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt).

name: Burning of Jan Hus
summary: The Bohemian preacher Jan Hus was condemned by the Council of Constance and burned at the stake on 6 July 1415.
body:
Part of [Council of Constance](event:council-of-constance). Jan Hus was a priest and rector of the university of Prague who preached in Czech at the Bethlehem Chapel against clerical wealth and the sale of indulgences, drawing on the writings of John Wycliffe.

He travelled to the council under a safe conduct from Sigismund, king of the Romans, was arrested soon after arriving, and was tried on articles drawn from his works. He refused to abjure positions he said he had never held, was declared a heretic and was burned outside the walls of Constance on 6 July 1415. His ashes were thrown into the Rhine.

The execution was received in Bohemia as a breach of faith by the king. Within four years it had led to the [Hussite Wars](event:hussite-wars), and Hus became a national figure; 6 July is a public holiday in the Czech Republic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hus).

name: Age of Discovery
summary: European ships opened sea routes to Africa, Asia and the Americas, joining the world's hemispheres into a single system.
body:
The Age of Discovery is the name given to the period, roughly from the early fifteenth century to the early seventeenth, in which European ships found and mapped sea routes to Africa, Asia and the Americas. It joined hemispheres that had been effectively separate since the end of the last ice age, and it began the European maritime empires.

Portugal started it, for reasons of position and of politics. The capture of Ceuta in 1415 gave a foothold in Morocco; from the 1420s expeditions sponsored by [Prince Henry](event:henry-navigator) worked south along the Atlantic coast of Africa, settling Madeira and the Azores and passing Cape Bojador in 1434, a limit sailors had believed impassable. Each voyage went a little further and came back with gold, pepper and enslaved people. The caravel, lateen-rigged and able to beat back north against the prevailing winds, made the return journey possible; the quadrant, the astrolabe and tables of solar declination made latitude calculable.

[Dias](event:dias) rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and [da Gama](event:da-gama) reached Calicut ten years later. [Columbus](event:columbus), sailing west for Spain on a serious underestimate of the size of the Earth, made landfall in the Bahamas in 1492 and never accepted that it was not Asia. [Magellan's expedition](event:magellan) crossed the Pacific, and one of its ships came home in 1522 having gone round.

The consequences differed by region. Europe gained world maps, new crops, bullion and a lead in armed shipping. In the Americas the voyages were followed by [conquest](event:spanish-conquest) and by [epidemics](event:americas-epidemics) that killed most of the population within a century. In Africa they were followed by four hundred years of the [Atlantic slave trade](event:slave-trade), and in Asia by armed European trading posts that later became colonies. The [Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange) of crops, animals and diseases changed diets and populations everywhere.

The voyages are listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery).

steps.name: Past Cape Bojador
steps.page: Cape Bojador, on the Saharan coast south of the Canaries, was where the Portuguese effort stopped for a decade. The current sets south and the wind blows south, so a ship that went beyond it might not get back, and sailors said the sea boiled there. Gil Eanes passed it in 1434 by standing out to sea and returning on a wide westward arc, the manoeuvre later called the *volta do mar*, which was used on every later Atlantic route.

steps.name: The Guinea coast
steps.page: After Henry's death the crown leased the African trade to merchants and then took it back. Ships reached the Gold Coast in the 1470s, where the fort of São Jorge da Mina was built in 1482 to hold the gold trade, and crossed the equator soon after. Diogo Cão found the mouth of the Congo in 1483. The coast was measured as it went: stone *padrões* were set up at the furthest point of each voyage, and the pilots' latitude tables were corrected once the Pole Star dropped below the horizon.

steps.name: Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
The Portuguese in the Indian Ocean
steps.page: Portugal followed the route with fleets. Cabral, blown or steered west on the way to India in 1500, made landfall in Brazil and claimed it. Afonso de Albuquerque then took the choke points rather than the territory: Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511, Hormuz in 1515, with an attempt on Aden that failed. It was a trading empire held by fortresses and gunnery, and for a century it controlled the sea route between Europe and Asia.

steps.name: The first circumnavigation
steps.page: Five ships under Ferdinand Magellan left Spain in 1519 to reach the spice islands by sailing west. They found the strait at the foot of South America, crossed a Pacific far wider than anyone had imagined, and lost most of their crews to starvation and scurvy; Magellan was killed in the Philippines. One ship, the *Victoria*, came home in 1522 under Juan Sebastián Elcano with eighteen men aboard, having sailed round the world and settled the argument about its size.

steps.name: The Pacific and the northern routes
steps.page: The return route across the Pacific was found in 1565, which made the Manila galleon possible and tied American silver to Chinese markets for two and a half centuries. English and Dutch ships entered waters the treaty of 1494 had assigned elsewhere: Drake went round the world between 1577 and 1580, and expeditions searched for north-west and north-east passages that did not exist in any usable form. By 1600 the outline of the inhabited world, apart from Australia and the Pacific interior, was on European charts.

name: Prince Henry the Navigator
summary: The Portuguese prince sponsored voyages down the Atlantic coast of Africa and the settlement of Madeira and the Azores.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Prince Henry of Portugal, called the Navigator by later English writers, sponsored the voyages that took Portuguese ships down the Atlantic coast of Africa in the middle of the fifteenth century. He never sailed on any of them. What he supplied was money, royal protection and persistence: expedition after expedition sent out from the Algarve until each obstacle in turn was passed.

He was a younger son of John I, took part in the capture of Ceuta in 1415, and afterwards held the governorship of the Order of Christ, whose revenues paid for much of the effort. From about 1420 his captains settled Madeira, and from 1427 the Azores. Cape Bojador, on the Saharan coast, was passed in 1434 by Gil Eanes at his second attempt, which broke a belief that nothing could return from beyond it. Ships reached the Senegal river and Cape Verde by 1444 and Sierra Leone by about 1460, the year Henry died.

The voyages were commercial from the start. Gold, malagueta pepper and enslaved Africans came back; the first cargo of captives was landed and sold at Lagos in 1444, and Portugal built from it a trade in enslaved people that it carried on for four hundred years.

The picture of Henry as a scholar presiding over a school of navigation at Sagres is a nineteenth-century invention. What is documented is a sustained programme of state-backed exploration, and the ship it produced, the caravel, which made the later [route to India](event:da-gama) possible.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Henry_the_Navigator).

name: Hussite Wars
