summary: A series of wars fought in Bohemia from 1419 to 1434 between the followers of Jan Hus and crusading armies raised by the pope and Sigismund of Hungary. Five crusades were defeated.
body:
The Hussite Wars were fought in the Bohemian lands between 1419 and 1434. On one side were the Hussites, followers of the Prague preacher Jan Hus, who had been burned as a heretic at the [Council of Constance](event:council-of-constance) in 1415. On the other were Sigismund of Hungary, heir to the Bohemian crown, and five crusades proclaimed against Bohemia by the papacy.

The Hussites demanded communion in both kinds for the laity, free preaching, the punishment of public sins and the end of the clergy's worldly possessions, set out as the Four Articles of Prague in 1420. They divided into a moderate party centred on Prague and the radical Taborites based at the new town of Tabor.

Their armies were commanded first by Jan Zizka and after his death in 1424 by Prokop the Great. They fought as infantry with crossbows and light cannon behind a laager of war wagons, which could stop armoured cavalry in the open field, and they made war pay by raiding the neighbouring lands. Each crusade in turn was defeated or dispersed.

The war ended between the Hussites themselves. At [Lipany](event:lipany) in 1434 the moderates and the Catholic nobles destroyed the Taborite field army, which opened the way to the Compacts agreed at Basel and accepted at Jihlava in 1436, allowing the Bohemian church its own usage under Sigismund.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite_Wars).

steps.name: The defenestration of Prague
steps.page:
On 30 July 1419 a procession led by the priest Jan Zelivsky attacked the New Town hall in Prague and threw the councillors from the windows. King Wenceslaus IV died on 16 August, leaving his brother Sigismund, king of the Romans and of Hungary, as heir.

Sigismund had given Jan Hus a safe conduct to the [Council of Constance](event:council-of-constance) four years earlier and had not prevented his burning, and the Bohemian estates refused to accept him. The Four Articles of Prague, issued in 1420, set out the Hussite demands.

steps.name: The first crusade and Vitkov Hill
steps.page:
Pope Martin V proclaimed a crusade in March 1420 and Sigismund reached Prague on 30 June with an army drawn from the empire and Hungary. On 14 July a small Hussite force under Jan Zizka held the fortified hill of Vitkov east of the city against an attack by the crusader cavalry.

The crusaders withdrew at the end of July. Sigismund was crowned in Prague castle but could not hold the city, and was beaten again at Vysehrad on 1 November. The Taborites had already won the first pitched battle of the war at Sudomer on 25 March.

steps.name: Kutna Hora and Nemecky Brod
steps.page:
Sigismund invaded from Moravia in December 1421 and took Kutna Hora, the silver town that paid for the Bohemian crown. Zizka, encircled there, broke out at night on 22 December behind a screen of war wagons and guns.

He turned on the retreating royal army in the first days of January and destroyed it at Nemecky Brod on 6 January 1422. The Hussite field armies fought around a mobile laager of wagons carrying crossbows and light cannon, a method built for infantry raised from towns and villages.

steps.name: Usti nad Labem
steps.page:
A Saxon and Meissen army came down the Elbe in June 1426 to relieve the town of Aussig, which the Hussites were besieging. On 16 June the Hussite army under Prokop the Great and Sigismund Korybut met it outside the town and destroyed it.

Zizka had died of plague in October 1424 and Prokop, a priest, had taken over the field armies. The victory opened the northern border and was followed by Hussite operations into Lusatia and Saxony.

steps.name: Tachov
steps.page:
The fourth crusade entered western Bohemia in July 1427 under Cardinal Henry Beaufort and Frederick of Brandenburg, coming from Bavaria and the Upper Palatinate. It besieged Stribro, and on the approach of the Hussite field armies it broke up on 4 August near Tachov.

The crusaders lost their guns and baggage. After 1427 no crusade held together long enough to bring the Hussites to battle on ground of its own choosing.

steps.name: The rides abroad
steps.page:
From 1428 the Hussite field armies carried the war outside Bohemia in expeditions the Czech sources call spanile jizdy, the fine rides. They went into Silesia, Lusatia, Saxony, Meissen, Franconia, Austria and Hungary, living off the country and taking contributions from towns.

In 1433 a force of about 7,000 men marched through the Neumark into Prussia, took Dirschau, and reached the Baltic near Danzig. The rides paid the armies and pressed the neighbouring princes, and they made the war a matter for the whole of central Europe.

steps.name: Domazlice
steps.page:
The fifth crusade crossed the border on 1 August 1431 under Frederick of Brandenburg and the papal legate Giuliano Cesarini. On 14 August, near Domazlice, the crusaders heard the Hussite wagons and the hymn of the approaching army and broke before contact.

The baggage, the guns and the legate's own bull were taken. On 15 October the Council of Basel invited the Hussites to negotiate, which is what the defeat had made unavoidable.

name: Aztec Empire
summary: The Triple Alliance ruled central Mexico from Tenochtitlan, a lake city of perhaps 200,000 people.
body:
The Aztec empire was the dominant power of central Mexico from 1428 until its destruction by Spanish and Indigenous forces in 1521. It was not a single state but a Triple Alliance of three city-states, [Tenochtitlan](event:tenochtitlan-founded), Texcoco and Tlacopan, which together broke the older power of Azcapotzalco and then extended tribute across most of the region, from the Gulf coast to the Pacific.

Conquest meant tribute rather than administration. A defeated city-state normally kept its ruler, its gods and its local government and paid in cloth, cacao, feathers, maize and labour on a schedule recorded in painted books; Aztec officials collected it, and garrisons stood only where the frontier was unsafe. Some neighbours were never conquered at all. Tlaxcala, an enemy state surrounded by imperial territory, later supplied the Spanish with most of their army.

The Mexica of Tenochtitlan built a city of perhaps 150,000 to 200,000 people on an island, fed by *chinampa* gardens and by tribute, with markets that astonished the Spanish and schools that took in commoners as well as nobles. Their religion required human sacrifice, chiefly of war captives, on a scale that is genuinely disputed but was certainly large; the "flower wars" fought with Tlaxcala supplied part of it.

Hernán Cortés landed in 1519 with about six hundred men and made allies of the empire's enemies. Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521, after a siege, a smallpox epidemic and the loss of most of its population. Mexico City was built on top of it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_Empire).

name: Joan of Arc
summary: A peasant girl claiming divine voices lifted the siege of Orléans and had the dauphin crowned at Reims; she was burned as a heretic two years later.
body:
Part of [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war). Joan of Arc was a peasant girl from Domrémy in Lorraine who, saying she was directed by the voices of saints, persuaded the disinherited French dauphin to give her a place with his army in 1429, helped raise the English siege of Orléans, and saw him crowned Charles VII at Reims. She was captured the following year, tried by a church court, and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431, aged about nineteen.

The French cause was close to lost when she appeared. Half the country was held by the English and their Burgundian allies, the Treaty of Troyes had disinherited the dauphin, and Orléans was the last barrier on the Loire. Joan was examined by theologians at Poitiers, given armour and a banner, and sent with a relief convoy. The siege was lifted in nine days; a run of victories along the Loire followed, and the army then marched three hundred kilometres through hostile country to Reims, where the coronation gave Charles the legitimacy the English had denied him.

She was taken outside Compiègne in May 1430 by Burgundians, who sold her to the English. The trial was conducted by a French bishop in English service on charges of heresy that turned largely on her wearing men's clothes and on her claim to be instructed by God directly. A papal court overturned the verdict in 1456.

The war was won without her. She was canonised in 1920 and is a patron saint of France.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc).

name: Battle of Lipany
summary: The Taborite field army was destroyed by a coalition of moderate Hussites and Catholic nobles on 30 May 1434, ending the Hussite Wars.
body:
Part of [Hussite Wars](event:hussite-wars). The battle was fought on 30 May 1434 near the village of Lipany, east of Prague, between the radical Taborite and Orphan field armies and a coalition of moderate Utraquist Hussites and Catholic Bohemian nobles.

The coalition attacked the wagon laager, then fell back in what the radicals took for a rout. The Taborites left their wagons to pursue and were caught in the open by the cavalry. Prokop the Great and Prokop the Lesser were both killed and the field armies ceased to exist.

The battle settled which Hussite party would make terms. The Compacts of Basel, accepted at Jihlava in July 1436, allowed the Bohemian church communion in both kinds and Sigismund was recognised as king. Tabor kept its own organisation until 1452.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lipany).

name: Inca Empire
summary: Tawantinsuyu ran 4,000 km along the Andes, bound by roads, terraces and knotted-string records, and without money, writing or the wheel.
body:
Tawantinsuyu, "the four parts together", was the largest state ever built in the Americas. From its capital at Cuzco it ran some 4,000 kilometres down the Andes, from southern Colombia to central Chile, and held perhaps ten to twelve million people. It reached that size in under a century, beginning with the campaigns of Pachacuti from about 1438, and was taken by a Spanish force of fewer than two hundred men in 1532–33.

It ran without money, markets, writing or the wheel. Labour itself was the tax: households owed the state a rotating obligation, the *mit'a*, which built the roads, terraces, storehouses and temples, and the state fed and clothed the workers from its own stores while they served. Accounts were kept on *khipu*, knotted and coloured cords whose numerical content is well understood and whose narrative content is not. Some 40,000 kilometres of road, with rope suspension bridges and relay runners, tied the whole together.

Conquest was often negotiated. Local lords who submitted kept their positions; those who did not were replaced, and whole populations were resettled as *mitmaq* colonists to break up resistance and to farm new ground. The state cult of the sun was imposed on top of local religion rather than in place of it.

A war of succession between Atahualpa and Huáscar, following an epidemic that had probably arrived ahead of the Spanish themselves, left the empire divided when Francisco Pizarro landed. Atahualpa was seized at Cajamarca in 1532 and executed in 1533; a rump Inca state held out at Vilcabamba until 1572.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire).

name: Gutenberg's printing press
summary: Gutenberg's movable metal type made books cheap and made it far harder to suppress an idea once it had spread.
body:
The printing press with movable metal type was assembled by [Johannes Gutenberg](item:johannes-gutenberg) at Mainz in the 1440s. Within fifty years presses were working in more than two hundred European towns and had produced something like twenty million books, more than all the scribes of the previous thousand years together.

No single part of it was new. [Block printing](event:woodblock-printing) had come from China, [metal type](event:korea-movable-type) had been cast in Korea two centuries earlier, and the screw press was borrowed from wine and oil making. What Gutenberg put together was a system: a hand mould that cast thousands of identical letters in a lead-tin-antimony alloy quickly and to a uniform height, an oil-based ink that would hold to metal instead of beading on it, and a press that applied even pressure across a whole forme at once. Each part had to work for the others to be worth anything.

A printed book cost a fraction of a manuscript, and the cost per copy fell with the length of the run, so printers had to find markets. They found them in universities, churches, courts, merchants' offices and eventually households. Latin gave way to the vernaculars as the audience widened; spelling and grammar hardened as texts were reproduced identically; title pages, page numbers, indexes and errata appeared because they had become useful.

Its political effect was that an idea in print could not be recalled. Luther's tracts made the [Reformation](event:reformation) a European event within months rather than a local dispute; identical diagrams and tables let natural philosophers across the continent build on one another's results, which the [Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution) required; and governments answered with censorship, licensing and privilege systems.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press).

name: Battle of Varna
summary: An Ottoman army under Murad II destroyed a Hungarian and Polish crusading force at Varna on the Black Sea on 10 November 1444. King Wladyslaw III was killed.
body:
Part of [Ottoman Empire](event:ottoman-empire). The crusade of Varna followed a successful Hungarian campaign in the Balkans in 1443 and the ten year truce of Szeged agreed in the summer of 1444. Under pressure from the papal legate Giuliano Cesarini and with promises of a Venetian fleet, Wladyslaw III of Poland and Hungary repudiated the truce and marched to the Black Sea coast.

Murad II crossed the straits with an army several times larger, the promised blockade of the Bosphorus having failed. The armies met outside Varna on 10 November 1444. The Hungarian wings held, but a charge by the king against the janissaries around the sultan ended with his death, and the army broke.

The defeat ended organised crusading against the Ottomans in the Balkans. Janos Hunyadi was beaten again at Kosovo in 1448, and no relief came to Constantinople when it was besieged in [1453](event:fall-constantinople).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Varna).

name: Pope Nicholas V and the early Renaissance
summary: The pope patronised humanists, collected manuscripts and began rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica, making Rome a centre of the Renaissance.
body:
Part of [The Renaissance](event:renaissance). Tommaso Parentucelli, pope as Nicholas V from 1447 to 1455, was the first humanist to hold the office, and the man who made Rome a centre of the [Renaissance](event:renaissance). He had spent his career as a scholar and a librarian before his election, and he spent his pontificate buying, copying and translating books, and rebuilding a city that a century of papal absence and schism had left half-ruined.

He came to the papacy at a favourable moment for it. The rival pope elected by the Council of Basel resigned in 1449, ending the last of the Western Schism, and the jubilee of 1450 brought pilgrims and their money to Rome in enormous numbers.

His agents bought manuscripts across Europe and in the Greek east, and he paid humanists, among them Lorenzo Valla, whose scholarship had recently embarrassed the papacy, to translate Herodotus, Thucydides, Strabo and Ptolemy into Latin. The collection of some 1,200 volumes he left is the foundation of the Vatican Library, formally established by his successor Sixtus IV.

He repaired the walls, bridges and aqueducts of Rome, restored its churches, and formed the plan of demolishing the crumbling fourth-century basilica of St Peter and building a new one, which his successors carried out over the next century and a half.

He also issued the bull *Dum Diversas* in 1452, authorising the Portuguese crown to reduce non-Christians to perpetual servitude. It is one of the documents on which the [Atlantic slave trade](event:slave-trade) was afterwards founded.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Nicholas_V).

name: Printing
summary: The reproduction of text and images by mechanical means, which made copies of a text cheap to produce in quantity.
body:
Printing is older than the printing press. [Woodblock printing](item:woodblock-printing) was in use in Tang China by the seventh century, and [movable type](item:korea-movable-type), ceramic under the Song and metal in Goryeo Korea by 1234, preceded Europe by two centuries. What limited them was the script: a font of Chinese characters runs to thousands of sorts, and a scribe was often the cheaper option.

An alphabet changes that arithmetic, and [Gutenberg's](item:johannes-gutenberg) combination of a type mould, oil-based ink and the [screw press](item:printing-press) made the copying of a book a matter of hours. The [42-line Bible](item:gutenberg-42-line) demonstrated it; by 1500 some 20 million volumes had been printed in Europe.

An idea in print could not be suppressed by burning one copy, which is part of why the [Reformation](item:reformation) spread as it did; standardised texts made the [Scientific Revolution's](item:scientific-revolution) accumulation of results possible; and fixed spellings and vernacular Bibles hardened national languages.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_printing).

name: Leonardo da Vinci
summary: Florentine painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks and few finished paintings define the range of the Italian Renaissance.
body:
Leonardo was the illegitimate son of a notary, apprenticed at about fourteen to Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence. He worked for the Sforza in Milan, for Cesare Borgia as a military engineer, for the Republic of Florence and finally for Francis I of France, who gave him a manor house near Amboise.

He finished very little. *The Last Supper* and the [*Mona Lisa*](item:mona-lisa) are among perhaps fifteen surviving paintings, and both changed how European artists handled gesture, atmosphere and the modelling of light.

His notebooks, some 7,000 surviving pages in mirror writing, range over anatomy from dissection, the flight of birds, water, geology, optics and machines from a diving suit to a helical rotor. Almost none of it was published in his lifetime, so its influence on later science was slight.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci).

name: Fall of Constantinople
summary: Ottoman cannon breached the Theodosian walls and the last Roman emperor died fighting; the Byzantine Empire ended after 1,100 years.
body:
Constantinople fell to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, after a siege of fifty-three days. The last Roman emperor, Constantine XI, was killed in the fighting and his body was never identified. The empire that had governed from the city since 330 ended with him, 1,123 years after Constantine I founded it.

The city had never recovered from the [Fourth Crusade's](event:fourth-crusade) sack in 1204, its territory had shrunk to the walls and a few outposts, and perhaps 50,000 people lived among fields and ruins in a city built for many times that. The Theodosian walls, though, had turned back every attacker for a thousand years.

Mehmed brought between 50,000 and 80,000 men against fewer than 8,000 defenders, and a siege train that included a bombard cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban which threw a stone ball of over half a tonne. The defence of the land walls was directed by the Genoese commander Giovanni Giustiniani. The siege ran in phases, from the first bombardment through the moving of a fleet overland into the Golden Horn to the assault of 29 May; the steps follow them in order.

Mehmed entered the city that day, allowed the customary three days of plunder and then stopped it early, and made Constantinople his capital. Hagia Sophia became a mosque. He repopulated the city by resettlement and confirmed the Orthodox patriarch in office as head of his Christian subjects.

Europe received the news as a catastrophe. It helped push Greek scholars and manuscripts west into the [Renaissance](event:renaissance), and Ottoman control of the land routes east is part of the reason European states began looking for [a sea route to Asia](event:age-of-discovery).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople).

steps.name: The army before the walls
steps.page:
Ottoman troops appeared before the land walls on 2 April 1453 and Mehmed II arrived with the main body on 5 April. Estimates of his army run from 50,000 to 80,000 men, against rather under 8,000 defenders for a perimeter of some twenty kilometres.

The defenders drew the great chain across the mouth of the Golden Horn, closing the harbour to the Ottoman fleet. Mehmed placed his own tent opposite the Mesoteichion, the middle stretch of wall where the Lycus stream crosses the line and the ground is lowest. Karaca Pasha took the northern sector, Ishak Pasha the ground from the Lycus down to the Marmara.

layers.label: The chain across the Golden Horn
Ottoman fleet at the Double Columns

steps.name: The bombardment opens
steps.page:
The siege proper began on 6 April, when the guns opened on the land walls. The largest was cast at Edirne by the Hungarian founder Orban and threw a stone ball of over half a tonne; it could be fired only a few times a day.

The batteries concentrated on the Mesoteichion and on the Charisius gate. Sections of the outer wall were brought down and rebuilt at night with earth, rubble and barrels, and the defenders held the repaired stockade rather than the breach. A general assault on 18 April was thrown back after several hours.

steps.name: Four ships reach the Horn
steps.page:
On 20 April three Genoese ships carrying men and supplies from the pope, and one imperial transport carrying grain, met the Ottoman fleet off the city. The Ottoman vessels were smaller and lower and could not board the tall Genoese carracks.

The fight was watched from both shores. The four ships worked through, the chain was opened to let them into the Golden Horn, and Mehmed removed the fleet commander Baltaoglu. The action showed that the harbour could not be forced while the chain held.

steps.name: Ships hauled into the Golden Horn
steps.page:
On 22 April Mehmed had about seventy vessels dragged out of the Bosphorus and hauled on greased rollers over the ridge behind Galata, then launched into the Golden Horn above the chain. The Genoese of Pera, formally neutral, did not stop the work.

A fleet inside the harbour put the low sea walls along the Horn under threat and forced the defenders to spread their small numbers further. An attempt to burn the ships with fire ships on 28 April failed, and the captured survivors were executed within sight of the walls.

steps.name: Mines and the siege tower
steps.page:
Between 16 and 25 May Ottoman sappers, many of them Saxon silver miners from Serbia, drove tunnels under the walls in the Blachernae sector. The defenders located them by countermining under the direction of the engineer Johannes Grant, and flooded, burned or fought them out underground.

A wheeled siege tower brought up against the Caligaria gate on 18 May was destroyed the following night. A partial lunar eclipse on 22 May and heavy rain in the days after were read in the city as omens.

steps.name: The last days
steps.page:
Mehmed offered terms which would have left Constantine XI a ruler in the Morea if the city were surrendered; the offer was refused. On 26 and 27 May the Ottoman camp prepared for a general assault, and fires were lit along the lines.

The defenders spent 28 May repairing the stockade at the Lycus and carrying icons in procession through the streets. A service was held in Hagia Sophia that evening, attended by both Orthodox and Latin clergy. The gates behind the outer wall were locked so that the garrison could not fall back.

steps.name: The final assault
steps.page:
The assault began shortly after midnight on 29 May and came in three waves: irregular azaps first, then Anatolian regiments, then the janissaries. The weight fell on the Mesoteichion, with attacks on the Blachernae walls and from the ships in the Horn.

Giovanni Giustiniani, who commanded the defence of the land walls, was wounded and carried off through the inner wall, and the stockade gave way behind him. A small postern, the Kerkoporta, was found open near Blachernae and Ottoman troops came through it. Constantine XI was killed in the fighting and his body was not identified. Mehmed entered the city that day and made it his capital.

name: Gutenberg Bible
summary: The first major book printed with movable type was a Latin Bible, made in Mainz in an edition of about 180 copies.
body:
Part of [Gutenberg's printing press](event:printing-press). The Gutenberg Bible, printed at Mainz and finished by 1455, is the first substantial book produced in Europe with movable metal type. It is called the 42-line Bible after the number of lines in most of its columns, and it is generally regarded as the object that proved the new technique could match the best manuscript work.

The edition was about 180 copies, roughly two-thirds on paper and the rest on vellum, which took the skins of several thousand calves. The text is the Latin Vulgate, set in a dense gothic type cut in imitation of the formal book hand of the Rhineland; the compositors used some 290 different sorts, including ligatures and abbreviated forms, in order to make the right-hand margin come out straight. The presses probably ran for about two years, with six of them working at once.

The books were sold unfinished. Initials, headings and any decoration were added by hand afterwards by rubricators and illuminators, so no two surviving copies look quite alike.

Gutenberg did not profit from it. His financier Johann Fust sued him as the work was completing, took the workshop and the type, and went into business with Gutenberg's foreman Peter Schöffer.

Forty-nine copies survive, of which twenty-one are complete. They are among the most valuable printed books in the world, and no complete copy has come on the market since 1978.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gutenberg_Bible).

name: Wars of the Roses
summary: A series of English civil wars between the houses of Lancaster and York, fought between 1455 and 1487. They ended with the victory of Henry Tudor at Bosworth and the Tudor dynasty.
body:
The Wars of the Roses were fought in England between 1455 and 1487 between supporters of the houses of Lancaster and York, both descended from Edward III. The name comes from the badges later attached to the two sides, a red rose for Lancaster and a white for York.

The background was the reign of Henry VI, who came to the throne as an infant, suffered a breakdown in 1453, and presided over the loss of the English lands in France at the end of the [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war). Government fell to competing groups of magnates with private armies raised by indenture.

The fighting came in short bursts separated by years of peace. Richard of York was killed at Wakefield in 1460; his son took the throne as Edward IV after Towton in 1461; Henry VI was briefly restored in 1470 and Edward recovered the crown at Barnet and Tewkesbury in 1471. After Edward's death in 1483 his brother took the throne as Richard III and his two nephews disappeared in the Tower.

Henry Tudor, a Lancastrian claimant through his mother, landed in Wales in 1485 and killed Richard at [Bosworth](event:bosworth). He married Elizabeth of York and put down the last Yorkist rising at Stoke Field in 1487.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_the_Roses).

steps.name: First St Albans
steps.page:
Richard, duke of York, and the Nevilles met the royal party in the streets of St Albans on 22 May 1455. Fewer than 160 men were killed, among them the duke of Somerset, the earl of Northumberland and Lord Clifford.

Henry VI was taken into York's keeping and York became protector for the second time. The quarrel was still about who advised the king rather than who should be king, and the deaths of three leading Lancastrians made it a blood feud between families.

steps.name: Northampton and Wakefield
steps.page:
The Yorkist earls returned from Calais in 1460, took Henry VI at Northampton on 10 July, and York claimed the throne itself in October. The Act of Accord left Henry king for life and made York his heir, disinheriting the prince of Wales.

Queen Margaret raised the north. On 30 December 1460 York left Sandal castle near Wakefield and was killed with his son Edmund; the earl of Salisbury was executed the next day. Their heads were set on the gates of York.

steps.name: Towton
steps.page:
York's heir Edward beat a Welsh Lancastrian force at Mortimer's Cross on 2 February 1461, while Margaret's northern army won the second battle of St Albans on 17 February and recovered the king. London shut its gates to her and admitted Edward, who was proclaimed king on 4 March.

The armies met in snow at Towton in Yorkshire on 29 March 1461, in what is usually called the largest battle fought on English soil. The Lancastrians were broken and Henry VI, Margaret and their son fled to Scotland.

steps.name: Warwick, the readeption and Barnet
steps.page:
Edward IV quarrelled with the earl of Warwick, who had made him king, over his marriage and over policy towards France. Warwick allied with Margaret, drove Edward abroad in 1470 and restored Henry VI to the throne.

Edward landed at Ravenspur in Yorkshire in March 1471, gathered support as he marched south and entered London. On 14 April he beat and killed Warwick in fog at Barnet. Margaret had landed the same day; on 4 May he destroyed her army at Tewkesbury, where her son Edward of Westminster was killed. Henry VI died in the Tower a few weeks later.

steps.name: Stoke Field
steps.page:
The last battle of the wars was fought at East Stoke near Newark on 16 June 1487. The Yorkist claimant was a boy, Lambert Simnel, presented as Edward, earl of Warwick, and crowned in Dublin. His backers landed in Lancashire with about 2,000 German mercenaries and an Irish contingent.

Henry VII's army broke them in about three hours. The earl of Lincoln was killed, Simnel was pardoned and put to work in the royal kitchens. Henry married Elizabeth of York in 1486, joining the two claims in his heirs.

name: Battle of Towton
summary: Fought in a snowstorm in Yorkshire on 29 March 1461, Towton is usually described as the largest battle ever fought on English soil. The Yorkist victory confirmed Edward IV as king.
body:
Part of [Wars of the Roses](event:wars-of-the-roses). The battle was fought on 29 March 1461, Palm Sunday, on a plateau between the villages of Towton and Saxton in Yorkshire. Edward IV had been proclaimed king in London three weeks earlier and marched north to make the claim good against the army of Henry VI and Margaret of Anjou.

Contemporary figures put both armies together at 50,000 or more, which modern historians reduce but still treat as exceptionally large for England. Snow blew into the Lancastrians' faces and shortened their arrows, and the Yorkist archers used the difference before closing.

The fighting lasted several hours and ended when the duke of Norfolk's men arrived on the Yorkist right. The Lancastrian line broke and many were killed in the flight across Cock Beck. A grave excavated at Towton Hall in 1996 held 38 men with severe head wounds, most of them healed veterans of earlier fighting.

Henry VI, Margaret and their son fled to Scotland. Edward was crowned in June.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Towton).

name: Songhai Empire
summary: The successor to Mali, Songhai became the largest empire in medieval West Africa before being conquered by Morocco.
body:
Songhai was the last and largest of the great empires of the West African Sahel. Based on the middle Niger at Gao, it took over the trade and much of the territory of [Mali](event:mali-empire) during the fifteenth century, and at its height controlled the river from beyond Timbuktu to the edge of modern Nigeria, an area larger than western Europe.

Sunni Ali, who ruled from 1464 to 1492, made it an empire. He built a river fleet, took Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné in 1473 after a long siege, and dealt harshly with the scholars of Timbuktu, who wrote the chronicles that survive and did not forgive him. His successor was overthrown in 1493 by a general who took the title Askia and ruled as Askia Muhammad until 1528, making the pilgrimage to Mecca, cultivating the scholars, and organising the empire into provinces under appointed governors with a standing army and a bureaucracy of Muslim officials behind them.

Timbuktu under Songhai was a centre of teaching. The Sankoré and Djingareyber mosques housed teachers of law, theology, grammar and astronomy, and a copying trade produced the manuscripts that are still being catalogued today.

In 1591 the sultan of Morocco sent about four thousand men, many of them armed with arquebuses, across the Sahara after the salt mines and the gold trade. At Tondibi the Songhai army, far larger but armed with spears and bows, broke under gunfire. The empire fell apart, the trans-Saharan trade declined, and no comparable state replaced it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songhai_Empire).

name: Onin War
summary: A civil war fought largely in and around Kyoto between 1467 and 1477 over the Ashikaga succession. It destroyed much of the capital and began the Sengoku period.
body:
The Onin War was fought from 1467 to 1477, mainly in Kyoto, between two coalitions of provincial governors led by Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sozen. The immediate question was the succession to the Ashikaga shogun Yoshimasa, who had named his brother as heir and then had a son.

The armies fought street by street through the capital for a decade, using arson and hired irregulars. Two thirds of Kyoto was burned, including most of the aristocratic quarters, and the imperial and shogunal households lost their revenues. Both original commanders died in 1473 and the fighting continued without an aim until the armies drifted home in 1477.

No side won and the war settled nothing, but the shogunate never recovered authority outside the capital. Provincial governors were displaced by local commanders who held land by force, a pattern known as gekokujo, the low overturning the high. Historians conventionally date the [Sengoku period](event:sengoku-unification) of warring states from 1467.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Cnin_War).

name: Spanish Inquisition
summary: A tribunal established in 1478 by Ferdinand and Isabella and controlled by the crown, charged with policing the orthodoxy of converts from Judaism and Islam. It was abolished in 1834.
body:
The Tribunal of the Holy Office of the Inquisition was established in Castile in 1478 by a papal bull issued at the request of Ferdinand and Isabella, and unlike earlier inquisitions it was appointed and controlled by the crown.

Its jurisdiction was over baptised Christians, so its first targets were conversos, Jews who had converted under the pressure of the pogroms of 1391 and after, who were suspected of practising Judaism in private. Jews who had not converted were expelled from Spain in 1492, the year [Granada](event:granada) fell; Muslims were required to convert or leave from 1502 in Castile, and the resulting moriscos were expelled between 1609 and 1614.

Procedure ran through denunciation, secret testimony, imprisonment and, in a minority of cases, torture, and ended in a public sentencing, the auto-da-fe. Modern archival studies count roughly 150,000 trials between 1480 and 1700 with something in the order of 3,000 to 5,000 executions, figures well below those given by earlier polemical literature.

The institution was suppressed under Napoleonic rule, restored, and finally abolished in 1834.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Inquisition).

name: Great Stand on the Ugra River
summary: Russian and Tatar armies faced each other across the Ugra river in the autumn of 1480 and withdrew without a battle. The episode is conventionally taken as the end of Moscow's tribute to the Horde.
body:
In 1480 Akhmat, khan of the Great Horde, marched against Moscow to enforce the tribute that Ivan III had stopped paying, and in alliance with Casimir IV of Poland and Lithuania. Ivan sent his forces to the line of the Oka and then the Ugra, a tributary that formed the border.

The two armies stood on opposite banks from late September, exchanging fire across the river and waiting for the ice. The Lithuanian army did not come, a Russian detachment raided the Horde's territory on the lower Volga, and both sides withdrew in November. Akhmat was killed by rivals the following January.

There was no battle, and historians treat the traditional date of 1480 for the end of the Tatar yoke as a convention rather than a break. Moscow had been acting independently for some years and continued to pay for peace with the Crimean khanate long afterwards. Ivan III went on to absorb Novgorod, Tver and Ryazan into a single Russian state.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Stand_on_the_Ugra_River).

name: Kingdom of Kongo
summary: A central African kingdom on the lower Congo river that entered into relations with Portugal in 1483, adopted Christianity, and was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade. Its central authority collapsed after the battle of Mbwila in 1665.
body:
The Kingdom of Kongo lay on the lower Congo river, in what is now northern Angola and the western Democratic Republic of the Congo, with its capital at Mbanza Kongo. It was governed by a king elected from a group of noble lineages and by provincial governors he appointed.

The Portuguese navigator Diogo Cao reached the river mouth in 1483. Diplomatic exchange followed, the king Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised in 1491, and his son Afonso I, who ruled from about 1509 to 1542, made Christianity the state religion, brought in Portuguese priests and craftsmen and corresponded with Lisbon and Rome. A Kongolese ambassador's son was consecrated bishop in 1518.

The same connection supplied captives to the Atlantic trade. Afonso wrote to the Portuguese king in 1526 asking that the traffic be limited to those lawfully enslaved and complaining that his own subjects were being taken. Kongo remained a major source of captives for Brazil for two centuries.

Portuguese forces from Angola defeated and killed the king Antonio I at Mbwila in 1665. The kingdom broke into rival factions and its capital was abandoned for a generation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kongo).

name: Battle of Bosworth Field
summary: Richard III was killed in Leicestershire on 22 August 1485 by the army of Henry Tudor, who became Henry VII. It was the last time an English king died in battle.
body:
Part of [Wars of the Roses](event:wars-of-the-roses). Henry Tudor landed at Mill Bay near Milford Haven on 7 August 1485 with about 2,000 men, most of them French, and marched through Wales and the west midlands gathering support. Richard III moved from Nottingham to Leicester and met him on 22 August near Ambion Hill in Leicestershire.

The Stanleys, with a substantial force, stood apart from both armies. When Richard led a mounted charge at Henry's standard and came close to reaching him, Sir William Stanley's men attacked Richard's flank. Richard was killed, the last English king to die in battle, and the crown was placed on Henry's head on the field.

Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in January 1486 and put down the last Yorkist rising at Stoke Field in 1487. Richard's remains were found under a car park in Leicester in 2012, identified by DNA in 2013 and reburied in the cathedral.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bosworth_Field).

name: Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
summary: Bartolomeu Dias led a Portuguese expedition that sailed around the southern tip of Africa, demonstrating a sea route to the Indian Ocean.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Bartolomeu Dias commanded the Portuguese expedition that rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488, proving that the Atlantic and Indian oceans connect and that a sea route from Europe to India existed. It was the decisive voyage of Portugal's seventy-year effort down the African coast.

He sailed from Lisbon in August 1487 with two caravels and a supply ship, following the coast south past the furthest point reached by Diogo Cão. Somewhere off present-day Namibia he stood out to sea, ran south before a storm for about two weeks out of sight of land, and then turned east to find nothing there; turning north instead brought him to the coast at Mossel Bay, well beyond the Cape. He had rounded Africa without seeing it.

He went on as far as the Great Fish River before his crews insisted on turning back. On the return he saw the Cape itself, and named it the Cape of Storms; King John II is said to have renamed it the Cape of Good Hope for what it promised. The voyage took sixteen months.

Dias did not command the expedition that followed it up. He helped fit out [Vasco da Gama's](event:da-gama) fleet and sailed with it as far as the Cape Verde islands, then joined Cabral's voyage to India in 1500, on which he was lost with four ships in a storm off the cape he had found.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomeu_Dias).

name: Fall of Granada
summary: The last Muslim emirate in Spain surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella; Jews were expelled from Spain the same year.
body:
Part of [The Reconquista](event:reconquista). Granada, the last Muslim state in the Iberian peninsula, surrendered to Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile on 2 January 1492. Its fall ended nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia and completed what later historians called the Reconquista.

The Nasrid emirate had survived as a tributary of Castile since 1238, protected by mountains, by fortifications and by the reluctance of Castilian kings to finish it. The union of Castile and Aragon in the marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella changed that arithmetic, and a civil war inside the Nasrid family gave them an opening. The war lasted ten years, from 1482, and was fought mostly as a series of sieges reduced by artillery; the emirate's towns fell one after another, and the city itself was starved out over the winter of 1491.

The Treaty of Granada promised the city's Muslims their property, their religion, their law and their language. The promise held for seven years. Forced conversions began in 1499, revolt followed, and by 1502 Islam was outlawed in Castile; the *moriscos*, the converted population and their descendants, were expelled from Spain altogether in 1609.

In the same year, 1492, the crown ordered the expulsion of every Jew who would not convert, ending a community that had lived in Iberia for more than a thousand years. The same monarchs gave [Columbus](event:columbus) his commission that year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War).

name: Columbus reaches the Americas
summary: Between 1492 and 1504 Christopher Columbus led four Spanish expeditions across the Atlantic to the Americas. The first made landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Between 1492 and 1504 the Italian explorer and navigator Christopher Columbus led four Spanish transatlantic expeditions to the Americas in the name of the Catholic Monarchs. On 12 October 1492, thirty-six days out from the Canary Islands, the first of them made landfall on an island in the Bahamas that Columbus named San Salvador. He believed he had reached the outlying islands of Asia and held to that view for the rest of his life, which is why the Caribbean came to be called the West Indies.

Columbus was looking for a western sea route to the East Indies and its spice trade. He took a small estimate of the circumference of the Earth and a large one of the eastward extent of Asia, and placed Japan about 4,500 kilometres west of the Canaries. Portuguese advisers rejected the calculation, correctly. After the [war for Granada](event:granada) ended, Isabella I and Ferdinand II agreed to fund the voyage on terms granting him the titles of admiral, viceroy and governor of any lands he found.

The first voyage left Palos de la Frontera in August 1492 with the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, visited the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola, and left thirty-nine men at La Navidad after the Santa María was wrecked on Christmas Day. The second, from 1493 to 1496, sailed with seventeen ships, founded La Isabela on Hispaniola and imposed tribute and forced labour on the Taíno. The third, from 1498 to 1500, reached Trinidad and the Orinoco delta, the first recorded European sighting of the South American mainland; complaints from colonists and reports of his government of Hispaniola led the crown to remove him as governor and send him back to Spain in chains. The fourth, from 1502 to 1504, followed the coast of Central America.

The Taíno population of Hispaniola fell steeply within a generation under warfare, forced labour and introduced disease. [Norse voyagers](event:vinland) had reached Newfoundland about five centuries earlier, but that contact did not continue. The voyages were followed by the [Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange), the [Spanish conquest of the mainland](event:spanish-conquest), the [epidemics](event:americas-epidemics) that killed most of the hemisphere's inhabitants, and sustained European colonisation of the Americas.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus).

name: The Columbian Exchange
summary: Crops, animals and diseases moved between the hemispheres after 1492, transforming diets and populations on every continent.
body:
The Columbian Exchange is the name given to the transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492. The historian Alfred Crosby coined the term in 1972. It is one of the largest biological events in human history, and its effects on diet and population were felt on every continent.

Disease moved chiefly in one direction. Smallpox, measles, typhus, influenza and later yellow fever entered populations with no acquired immunity to any of them and killed, on most estimates, between two thirds and nine tenths of the pre-contact population of the Americas within a century and a half. That collapse is inseparable from the European conquests: the [epidemics](event:americas-epidemics) ran ahead of the armies in many places, and the states that fell had often already lost their rulers and much of their administration.

Food crops moved chiefly the other way. Maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, beans, tomatoes, peppers, squash, cacao, groundnuts, pineapple and tobacco were unknown outside the Americas in 1491. Potatoes and maize yield far more calories per hectare than the grains they came to supplement in Europe, Africa and China, and the population growth of the following centuries, which supplied the workforce of the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution), depended on them. Cassava and maize became staples across much of Africa.

Traffic in the other direction included wheat, rice, sugar cane, bananas, coffee, cattle, pigs, sheep, chickens and the horse, which transformed societies on the plains of both American continents. Sugar and coffee were then grown in the Americas by enslaved Africans carried across in the [Atlantic slave trade](event:slave-trade).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange).

name: Treaty of Tordesillas
summary: Spain and Portugal drew a line across the world, dividing newly found lands between them.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). By the Treaty of Tordesillas, signed on 7 June 1494, Spain and Portugal divided the world outside Europe between themselves along a meridian in the Atlantic. Everything found west of the line was to be Castile's and everything east of it Portugal's. It is the first attempt to partition the globe by treaty, and it is the reason Brazil speaks Portuguese.

The occasion was [Columbus's return](event:columbus) in 1493. Pope Alexander VI, a Spaniard, issued bulls granting Castile the lands west of a line a hundred leagues beyond the Azores and Cape Verde islands. Portugal, which had spent seventy years opening the African route and held a prior treaty of its own, rejected this, and the two crowns negotiated directly instead. The compromise moved the line to 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands.

Nobody could measure longitude at sea, so where the line actually fell was guesswork, and it was never surveyed. Its practical effect was to leave the eastern bulge of South America on the Portuguese side, which Cabral reached in 1500. A companion agreement at Zaragoza in 1529 drew a second line on the far side of the world, through the Pacific.

The other European powers ignored the division as soon as they had ships to ignore it with; Francis I of France is supposed to have asked to see the clause in Adam's will that divided the world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Tordesillas).

name: Italian Wars
summary: A series of wars fought mainly in Italy between 1494 and 1559, in which France, Spain and the Habsburg emperors competed for the Italian states. They ended with Spanish predominance in Italy, confirmed at Cateau-Cambresis.
body:
The Italian Wars were fought between 1494 and 1559, mostly on Italian ground, between France on one side and Spain and the Habsburg emperors on the other, with the Italian states, the papacy, England, the Swiss and the Ottomans entering and leaving the alliances.

They began when Charles VIII of France invaded to claim Naples in 1494 and marched the length of the peninsula almost unopposed. Italy at the time was divided among Milan, Venice, Florence, the Papal States and Naples, wealthy and militarily weaker than the new national monarchies.

The wars are a standard marker in military history. Mobile siege artillery ended the medieval defensive advantage of high walls, which was answered by the low, angled bastion of the trace italienne; pike and arquebus formations displaced heavy cavalry as the decisive arm, as at [Pavia](event:battle-of-pavia) in 1525, where Francis I was captured.

The [sack of Rome](event:sack-of-rome) in 1527 by mutinous imperial troops is often taken as the end of the High [Renaissance](event:renaissance) in the city. The Peace of Cateau-Cambresis in 1559 left Spain holding Milan, Naples, Sicily and Sardinia, an arrangement that lasted until the eighteenth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Wars).

steps.name: Charles VIII marches on Naples
steps.page:
Charles VIII of France crossed the Alps in September 1494 with about 25,000 men and a train of bronze field guns, claiming the throne of Naples through the Angevin line. He passed through Turin and Pavia, entered Pisa on 8 November, Florence on 17 November and Rome on 31 December.

Naples was taken in February 1495 with almost no fighting; the fortress of Monte San Giovanni, which had once held out for seven years, fell in a few hours to the new artillery. The speed of the march is what alarmed the other Italian states and brought them into the League of Venice in March.

steps.name: Fornovo
steps.page:
The League of Venice put an army under Francesco Gonzaga across the French line of retreat at Fornovo di Taro, on the northern side of the Apennines, on 6 July 1495. Charles had left half his force in Naples and had about 10,000 men.

The French pushed their way across the Taro and reached Asti, losing the baggage train with the loot of the campaign. Both sides claimed the victory. Naples was lost again within the year, and the French kept coming back to Italy for the next sixty years.

steps.name: Agnadello and the League of Cambrai
steps.page:
The League of Cambrai of 1508 joined France, the Empire, Spain and the papacy against Venice, which had taken territory in Romagna and the Po valley. On 14 May 1509 Louis XII destroyed the Venetian field army at Agnadello, east of Milan.

Venice lost its mainland empire within weeks and then recovered most of it as the league broke up. The papacy changed sides against France, and by 1513 the alliances had reversed twice. The pattern of the wars was set: coalitions formed against whichever power was winning.

steps.name: Marignano
steps.page:
Francis I came to the throne in 1515 and crossed the Alps by a track through the Col de l'Argentiere that the Swiss holding the passes had not covered. On 13 and 14 September he fought the Swiss confederate army at Marignano, south east of Milan.

The battle ran into the night and was decided the next morning when Venetian troops arrived. The Swiss withdrew in order, having lost heavily. France recovered Milan, and the confederation signed the perpetual peace of 1516 and stopped fighting as a power in its own right.

steps.name: Saint-Quentin and the peace
steps.page:
The last round of the wars was fought largely outside Italy. A Spanish army under Emmanuel Philibert of Savoy beat the French at Saint-Quentin in Picardy on 10 August 1557; France took Calais from England the following January.

Both crowns were bankrupt, Spain and France each having suspended payments in 1557, and they made peace at Cateau-Cambresis on 3 April 1559. France kept Calais and the three bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun and gave up its claims in Italy, leaving Milan and Naples to Spain.

name: Vasco da Gama reaches India
summary: Da Gama opened the first sea route from Europe to India, breaking the Venetian and Ottoman monopoly on the spice trade.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on the Malabar coast of India on 20 May 1498, having left Lisbon the previous July. It was the first voyage from Europe to India by sea, and it opened a route that took the spice trade out of the hands of the middlemen who had carried it overland.

Rather than follow the African coast, da Gama's four ships stood far out into the South Atlantic to pick up the westerlies, a swing of some 6,000 kilometres out of sight of land and about ninety days at sea, much longer than [Columbus's](event:columbus) crossing. They rounded the Cape in November, worked up the East African coast past Mozambique and Mombasa, and at Malindi took on a pilot who knew the monsoon crossing to India.

Calicut produced little. Da Gama's gifts of cloth, hats, sugar and honey were of small value at a court accustomed to merchants trading in gold and silk, and the Muslim traders already established there had no reason to assist a competitor. He left with a small cargo and no treaty, and lost more than half his men to scurvy on the way home. The cargo still sold for many times the cost of the voyage.

Portugal followed it up with armed fleets. Da Gama himself returned in 1502 with twenty ships, bombarded Calicut and massacred the crew and passengers of a pilgrim vessel, establishing by force the pattern of Portuguese trade in the Indian Ocean for the next century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama).
